Lacy THE VULGATE AND POST-VULGATE CYCLES During the second half of the twelfth century, Chrétien de Troyes developed and fixed the form of the Arthurian episodic romance. In the process he popularized King Arthur in French, as Geoffrey of Monmouth had done in Latin, but he also contributed to the legend new characters and themes unknown to Geoffrey. These include in particular the love story of Lancelot and Guenevere and the quest for the Grail. Several texts, notably the works of Robert de Boron, from the end of that century, transformed the mysterious Grail into the “Holy Grail,” the Chalice of the Last Supper and the vessel in which Christ’s blood was collected after the crucifixion. Then, between 1215 and about 1235, an anonymous author or group of authors composed the Lancelot-Grail Cycle (also called the Vulgate Cycle, the Prose Lancelot, or the PseudoMap Cycle) of Arthurian romance. This cycle of five imposing romances can only be termed monumental, owing in equal measure to its enormous length, its complexity and literary value, and its influence. The romances run to several thousand pages of text, and they offer many hundreds of characters and countless adventures intricately interlaced with one another. Most important, they constitute the most extended attempt to elaborate the full story of the Arthurian era and to set that era in a framework of universal history. The two romances that stand first chronologically were actually composed after the other three. The Estoire del saint Graal (translated in this set as The History of the Holy Grail) opens the cycle by tracing the early history of the Grail, from Joseph of Arimathea to his son Josephe, who becomes the first Christian bishop, and eventually to Alain, the first Fisher King, who places the Grail in Corbenic Castle and begins the wait for the arrival of the chosen Grail Knight. The Story of Merlin depicts the role of the seer and magician in Arthur’s conception and birth, in his designation as king following the Sword in the Stone revelation, and in the establishment of the Round Table, a replica of the Grail Table (itself modeled after the table of the Last Supper). Merlin also directs Arthur’s major victories over his rebellious barons. These two romances are followed chronologically (but preceded in order of composition) by the Lancelot Proper, La Queste del saint Graal (The Quest for the Holy Grail), and La Mort Artu (The Death of Arthur). The first of these, constituting fully half of the entire cycle, presents Lancelot’s youth, his love for Guenevere, and a long series of exploits that he performs in her service. The second depicts the Grail Quest undertaken by a number of knights (Gawain, Bors, Perceval, and others) but finally accomplished by the chosen hero, Galahad. Concluding the cycle, The Death of Arthur traces the tragic decline and dissolution of the Arthurian world, due in large part to the sin of Lancelot and Guenevere, and closes with an account of the death of the king. The Vulgate Cycle was soon followed by an anonymous Post-Vulgate, based on the earlier cycle but characterized by the omission of the Lancelot Proper and, consequently, of the empha sis on Lancelot and Guenevere. The second cycle thus focuses squarely on the Grail quest and related pious themes. It includes versions of the other four romances represented in the Vulgate and even borrows the text of the Merlin intact; on the other hand, the Post-Vulgate Death of Arthur romance is a significantly abridged adaptation of its model. Without a Lancelot Proper, the second cycle is far shorter than the first, but it remains daunting nonetheless in its dimensions and in its complexity. The Post-Vulgate Cycle is further complicated for modern scholars and readers—and this is a complication almost beyond resolution—by the fact that some portions of the Old French text have long since disappeared, whereas others have survived only in fragments or in translations into Portuguese and Spanish. Extraordinary scholarly efforts, especially by Fanni Bogdanow, have made it possible to reconstitute significant portions of the texts. The importance of the Vulgate Cycle and, to a only slightly lesser extent, of the Post-Vulgate is almost incalculable. Portions of them (most often the Vulgate Lancelot-Quest—Death of Arthur) were translated or adapted into a number of other languages. Authors rendered much of the Vulgate narrative into German and Dutch, while the Quest was translated into Irish and Welsh. Italian and Hispanic authors too translated it or drew on it, although, as suggested, the PostVulgate proved more influential on the Iberian Peninsula than did the Vulgate. But for English-speaking readers, the importance of the Vulgate is indicated most clearly by its influence on Sir Thomas Malory, who took the cycle as the principal of his numerous sources: although each part of his work has multiple sources, his first, third, sixth, seventh, and eighth tales were drawn largely or principally from the Vulgate Cycle. He even gave his work, Le Morte Darthur, a title that indicates his indebtedness not only to related English romances like the Alliterative Morte Arthure and the Stanzaic Le Morte Arthur but to the final component of the Old French cycle. E. Jane Burns’s introduction offers a much more detailed presentation of the cycles, concentrating on content, authorship, techniques, and meaning. (A separate introduction to the Post-Vulgate will be included in Vol. IV.) NOTES CONCERNING THE TRANSLATIONS Owing in large part to the cycles’ length (and to no small degree to the inadequate editions of some of the texts), until now only a small fraction of the material has been translated. The only romances to have been translated in their entirety are the two shortest: the Quest and the Death of Arthur. A few scattered ex- Preface cerpts of the other romances are available in English. These volumes thus present the full cycles to modern readers for the first time. Malory scholars, whose need provided the initial impetus for this translation, will now have access to texts that are crucial to their work; they and others will also discover fascinating romances, each one distinctive in focus and narrative method but intricately linked to the others by themes that are continued, in interlaced form, from one romance to the next. The full set will comprise five volumes, in which the material is divided as follows: J. a. Introduction, by E. Jane Burns. b. The History of the Holy Grail, translated by Carol J. Chase c. The Story of Merlin, translated by Rupert T. Pickens II. a. Lancelot, part I translated by Samuel N. Rosenberg b. Lancelot, part II translated by Carleton W. Carroll c. Lancelot, part III translated by Samuel N. Rosenberg III. a. Lancelot, part IV translated by Roberta L. Krueger b. Lancelot, part V translated by William W. Kibler c. Lancelot, part VI translated by Carleton W. Carroll IV. a. The Quest for the Holy Grail, translated by E. Jane Burns b. The Death of Arthur, translated by Norris J. Lacy c. The Post-Vulgate, beginning, translated by Martha Asher . The Post-Vulgate, continued, translated by Martha Asher b. Chapter summaries for both cycles c. Rosenberg The fact that the nine translators are affiliated with nine separate institutions has naturally complicated the process of discussing and resolving editorial and translation problems. That process was materially aided by a major grant from the National Endowment for the Humanities, which, in addition to providing released time and other assistance, enabled the entire team to meet for several days on two occa- Preface sions. Most of the translators were also able to gather for discussions during three different meetings of the Medieval Institute of Western Michigan University. A good deal of the work, however, had to be done by mail, electronic mail, phone, and fax. The translator whose name is attached to each text retains final responsibility for that portion of the work, of course. In addition, at least one other member of the translation team has read each part for accuracy, and the general editor has read and edited the entire text to ensure reasonable consistency of approach from text to text and, especially, within the Lancelot Proper, the only romance that is the work of a number of translators. To make the Vulgate romances accessible to our audience, we have divided them into numbered and titled sections or chapters. Summaries of all romances, keyed to the chapter divisions, are included in the final volume. Notes give information about textual and cultural matters and offer a key to internal cross-references. The first note in each section indicates which pages of the translator’s principal source or sources are included in that section. Locating a particular passage in the Old French is made even easier by the insertion of a bracketed page number every time the translator begins a new page of the original. Each text, of course, has a distinct style and thus presents its own problems for translators. Writing of the last three romances of the Vulgate Cycle, Alfred L. Kellogg (in Chaucer, Langland, Arthur, Rutgers University Press, 1972, p. 11), describes the Lancelot Proper as “immense and brightly colored,” underlines the “emphatic piety” of the Quest, and characterizes the Death of Arthur as “compact, sober.” We have made every effort to respect and translate stylistic differences from romance to romance. We have also taken as our common purpose the need to respect both the medieval originals and the demands of contemporary English style. We have thus made a reasonable attempt to __avoid archaism, except where the Old French passage itself is archaic. The qualification here, indicated by “reasonable,” reflects our conviction that, without being intentionally archaic, the Old French romances were recognized by their readers as being fundamentally “unreal.” That is, the audiences who read these texts in a) the thirteenth century surely took them as a highly fictionalized account of a remote past that may or may not have existed. The translators’ problem in such a situation is thus to walk a thin line between a style and vocabulary that tend to update the texts and cast them in a pseudo-realistic mold and a style that, conversely, situates the romances clearly in a “fairy tale” world. We have therefore avoided modern colloquialisms, although we have not hesitated to use direct, matter-of-fact translations when they accurately render the flavor of the original. Other stylistic features of the romances require comment. First of all, the Old French texts tend to offer sequences of personal pronouns with little regard for noun referents. An example from the Merlin reads, in literal translation, “He had come so close to him that he could not get away from him, and he saw such a great number of men coming behind him that the whole field was clothed with them, and he saw clearly that if he stood his ground against him, he would put himself in great danger of being killed.” Although Old French style, unlike that of English, permits such a construction, the referents are occasionally obscure. Whenever the English translation is unclear, or even when such sentences are clear but nonetheless distracting, we have substituted the appropriate nouns for one or more pronouns. Thirteenth-century narrative style tends to be highly redundant. Texts often double or triple adjectives that present little or no distinction of meaning: typical examples, drawn from the History of the Holy Grail, include “he was frightened and afraid,” “nothing could make her joyful, happy, or content,” and “he could not see or perceive. .. .” We have retained a number of these expressions, for they convey the flavor of the original, but since English tolerates them far less well than does Old French, we have eliminated a good many examples. Some of the Vulgate texts, and especially the History of the Holy Grail, are redundant in another sense as well: passages have a tendency to “double back” on themselves, emphasizing narrative progression and consequence by structures such as “He opened the book. After he had opened the book... .” We have greatly reduced the number of such repetitions, since they quickly become intrusive and tiresome in English. Again, however, as they are a pervasive xu and characteristic feature of the History of the Holy Grail, we have kept as many of them as English style will support. We have dealt freely with a number of Old French rhetorical devices, such as typical statements of the kind, “He was so strong that no one could have been stronger.” We have reduced that, in most cases, to “he was the strongest man in the world” or “no one could have been stronger than he” or “he was as strong as could be.” Such modifications we have taken as nothing more than the normal procedures required to move a composition from one language to another. On the other hand, there are some expressions and structures that we have taken as essential elements of the authors’ rhetorical texture and have consequently retained. One is the expression, very common in Old French narrative, “then you could have seen/heard . . .”; for example, “when Lancelot rode into battle, you could have seen knights struck down left and right.” Although the sense of the passage is rendered equally well by “when Lancelot rode into battle, knights fell left and right” or “Lancelot rode into battle and struck down knights left and right,” neither translation retains the original’s sense of a relationship between a narrator and his audience. Some of the geographical locations cited in the text are real; thus, Norhomberlande or Norhombellande indisputably refers to Northumberland; in this and similar cases, we have used the familiar modern form of the name. On the other hand, a number of such locations are obviously imaginary. In a few cases, there is serious doubt about the reference: Carduel is often taken as Carlisle, for example, and Taneborc may be Edinburgh, but the identifications are by no means certain. In such instances, we have generally retained the Old French form rather than risk misleading the reader. We have dealt with characters’ names by translating their descriptive element. For example, we might have kept the form “Yvain le Grand,” which sounds perfectly acceptable. But in fact, “le Grand” means something specific, and we have preferred to present that meaning to our readers; the character in question is thus “Yvain the Tall.” Preface As indicated above, the translators have tried to steer a middle course. Our primary concern was to present a reliable and readable text to modern readers, but we have also made an effort to retain a certain number of the stylistic features of the Old French romances, provided those features were reasonably compatible with the characteristics of modern English usage. THE HISTORY OF THE HOLY GRAIL AND THE STORY OF MERLIN The History of the Holy Grail, far more than most texts of the period, has a convoluted, dense style that, at times, can only be described as turgid. In the Vulgate Cycle, only the Quest approaches it in terms of stylistic density and redundancy; moreover, if the Quest, as Kellogg suggested, demonstrates “emphatic piety,” the History of the Holy Grail is more emphatic and scarcely less pious, though considerably less graceful and subtle. The author appears to be far more concerned with substance and symbolism—everything possesses symbolic meaning, and everything is explicated in detail—than with concision and grace. At times, the text advances with acceptable ease, but often it frankly plods. Although, by necessity, the translator has in some cases presented a text that is clearer and more accessible than the original, we have thought it important to retain enough of the characteristics of the Old French to give a clear notion of the style and, particularly, of the stylistic distinctions between the History of the Holy Grail and the texts that follow it. In one crucial way, the two texts translated in this volume present common problems: neither translator was able to work from a single, authoritative critical edition. Rupert Pickens has based his translation of the Merlin primarily on the Sommer text, emending where necessary from manuscript variants and from Micha’s edition (which covers roughly the first eighty pages of the Sommer text). With the History of the Holy Grail in particular, the translator must deal with textual difficulties: the early Hucher edition has been the standard text, but it is entirely unreliable; Sommer offers little improvement, while the recent and generally superior Ponceau edition is still unpublished. Thus, to a good extent, Carol Chase has found it necessary to establish a Preface text as she translates the work. She worked primarily from Hucher but emended that text freely by referring to Sommer, to manuscript variants given by Hucher, and to the Ponceau thesis. Because our translations are intended to meet the needs of scholars as well as students and more general readers, notes offer information not only about cultural and literary matters but, especially for the History of the Holy Grail, about textual questions and the process of text construction. Jane Burns The Arthurian Vulgate Cycle lacks focus, rambles, gives you a headache, and puts you to sleep. Such were the observations of the seventeenth-century epic poet Chapelain, one of the cycle’s earliest commentators.! These remarks come from a reader who expects to find in the Arthurian prose romance of the thirteenth century a post-Cartesian logic wholly foreign to literary works of the High Middle Ages. But if Chapelain’s remarks can be dismissed as the naive product of an era long past, echoes of them ring loudly in the assessments of more contemporary critics. Many literary historians in our own century have mistakenly sought in Arthurian romance a recognizable ancestor text for the modern novel since the same French word, roman, designates extended narratives of both periods. Disappointment at not finding in the Vulgate Cycle a viable precursor for nineteenth-century literary sensibilities is often registered in comments decrying the cycle’s lack of unity, claims that these prose romances constitute one of the most disjointed European literary works ever written,? or that their highly repetitive narrative structure creates a monotony bordering on the offensive.* It is certainly true that the complex amalgam of five Arthurian tales constituting the Vulgate Cycle does not present the modern reader with an easily definable “text.” The corpus can be sectioned, on one level, into independent tales that begin chronologically with the Prose Lancelot 1Albert Pauphilet, Le Legs du Moyen Age (Melun: Librairie d’Argences, 1950), 30. 2J.D. Bruce, The Evolution of Arthurian Romance (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins Press, 1923), 410. 3Ferdinand Lot, Etude sur le “Lancelot en prose” (Paris, 1918, rpt. Paris: Champion, 1954), 63-64. This statement is especially significant since it comes from one of the cycle’s most ardent defenders. But after great effort to prove unity for the entire cycle, even Lot concedes reluctantly that coherence does not prevail. See also p. 262. XU (1215-20), a protracted story of the chivalric exploits undertaken by the quintessential knightlover whose adulterous liaison with Guenevere will subsequently cost his success on the Grail quest. This account prepares us for the Queste del Saint Graal (“Quest for the Holy Grail,” 1220-25) in which Perceval and Bors undertake the Grail adventure alongside the chosen hero Galahad, who is Lancelot’s spiritually pure son. But Lancelot’s continued adultery with the queen unleashes an inexorable chain of tragic events— narrated in La Mort le Roi Artu (“The Death of King Arthur,” 1225-30)—that culminate in a final holocaust on Salisbury Plain, where King Arthur and his bastard son Mordred kill each other. These three tales are preceded in terms of narrative chronology by two others that were actually composed after the initial Lancelot-Grail trilogy. The Estoire del Saint Graal (“The Story/ History of the Holy Grail,” after 1230) tells of the transfer of the Grail vessel from the Holy Land to Great Britain and subsequent miracles it performs there, and the Estoire de Merlin (“The Story/History of Merlin,” after 1230) chronicles the marvelous feats of the prophet-enchanter responsible for Arthur’s conception, his rise to power, and his exceptional military victories. The unwieldy mix of spiritual and chivalric modes that crisscross unevenly throughout this protracted prose narrative mark the Vulgate Cycle as a product of the emergent social and political tensions in thirteenth-century France. The rise of French vernacular literature in the mid-twelfth-century that had popularized chivalric tales about King Arthur and the knights of the Round Table underwent a significant shift around 1200 as the standard Arthurian adventure story was infused with Biblical allusion and the religious mystery of the Holy Grail. As verse accounts of courtly love and prowess, once delivered orally, were recast into prose narratives, possibly destined to be read, appeal was made xu simultaneously to two authoritative written traditions: historical chronicle and the Divine Book. Latin prose previously had been the medium for Geoffrey of Monmouth’s pseudo-history of the British kings, which featured, among many monarchs, the legendary King Arthur. Vernacular prose had formerly been used for religious purposes—in sermons, psalters, translations of Latin religious texts, and indeed the Bible itself (first translated into Old French at the beginning of the thirteenth century). Prose thus carried for many medieval authors a truthtelling value absent from the rhetorical artifice of purely literary verse accounts that by the thirteenth century were sometimes condemned as “vain pleasures.” Lady readers, in particular, were exhorted after 1200 to abandon the deceptive tales of Arthurian knights in favor of texts that would provide a more accurate and edifying truth.4 If the Christianization of Arthurian legend was encouraged by Church officials who, in the spirit of Thomas Aquinas’s Summa theologica later in the century (1274), sought to harmonize the sacred and secular worlds within totalizing systematic interpretations, that Christianization of a distant Arthurian past also served the political aspirations of the new Norman dynasty. King Henry II of England who first sought to legitimate his power by proclaiming the historical King Arthur as a revered ancestor, may also have cultivated around 1191 claims issued by the monks of Glastonbury that the tombs of Arthur and Guenevere had been “discovered” in the abbey church and that the Holy Grail had, according to their reading of Robert de Boron’s Joseph of Arimathea (ca. 1200), been transferred from the Holy Land to Glastonbury. Initially, the myth of a Christianized Arthur would have provided the Norman kings with a heroic ancestor figure to rival that of Charlemagne on the Continent. But by the time of the Vulgate Cycle’s composition, the Arthurian prose romances offered a model of comportment to the feudal aristocratic class, one that attempted to combine the irreconcilable interests of earthly chivalry and military conquest with the spiritual quest for peace. That attempt may reflect the struggle of the lesser nobles to carve out a place 4Daniel Poirion, Précis de la littérature francaise du Moyen Age (Paris: Presses Universitaires de France, 1978) , 94. Introduction for themselves among the competing interests of the higher, landed aristocracy on the one hand and the Church on the other. But what the Vulgate Cycle charts more than synthesis is the ongoing struggle of an impossible task. Through its seemingly endless proliferation of chivalric adventures, its repeated narrative expansions and extensions, its elaborate genealogies of ancestors, origins, and putative authors, this wandering, disjointed narrative records a struggle without resolution, a struggle— characteristic of many literary and philosophical texts of the thirteenth century in France—to give a comprehensive account on an enormous scale, the very size of which might somehow tie competing and disparate elements together. Known by many titles, the Arthurian Vulgate Cycle derives its most common name from the first—and the only complete—edition of the cycle, undertaken by H. Oskar Sommer between 1908 and 1912.5 French scholars speak typically of the Lancelot-Grail Cycle, although this appellation does not include the Merlin and sometimes omits the Estoire® Attribution of the Lancelot, the Queste, and the Mort Artu to Walter Map has fostered occasional reference to the whole corpus as the Pseudo-Map Cycle. The titles hold one key word in common; all refer to a “cycle” of tales, depicting thereby an expansive narrative structure that generates a textual corpus of uncertain dimensions. Unity does not rank high on this compositional agenda. Are we dealing with one composite work or a set of relatively autonomous and individualized tales? And who or where is the author responsible for their composition? The cycle’s earliest commentators struggled tirelessly with just such questions. Indeed, their frustration with the Vulgate’s rambling narrative style was often exacerbated by an uneasiness concerning the anonymous status of these and so many other Old French texts. Chapelain’s exasperated assessment of the Vulgate Cycle as a literary “dungheap” in which one might locate a few textual diamonds, led to the inevitable conclusion that the work’s author must have been a barbarian.® Later critics, who more accurately attributed the Vulgate’s lack of focus to an unmonitored succession of authors and redactors,? expressed an equally acute dismay at the absence of a known author’s governing hand. Whereas Chapelain rejects the cycle as formless, concluding that this literary voyage is not worth the trip, Lot and his followers provide a map for effectively charting the unwieldy romance terrain. Through the theories of entrelacement (or narrative interlace) and consistent chronology advanced in his Etude sur “le Lancelot en prose,” for example, Lot makes the disparate landscapes of the Vulgate Cycle navigable for the uninitiated or skeptical reader (pp. 17-28, 29-64) .12 He shows in essence how the seemingly random mingling of individual chivalric adventures actually follows a consistent and logical plan. As the conte, the “story” or narrative line, switches furtively from detailing the exploits of Lancelot to following the adventures of Bors or describing the deeds of Gawain, the apparent narrative chaos is anchored in a clear chronology of dates and times. We follow the principal characters day by day and hour by hour along twisting paths that actually conform to a surprisingly rigorous calendar of events. The precise correlation of names and dates supplies a tangible record of the author’s mindful participation in the tale. They serve as footprints leading us back to his former and formative presence. Lot’s analysis attenuates and legitimates the randomness of the adventure story by attributing it to a hypothetical author deemed as conscientious as a Beaumarchais, Scribe, or Sardou (p. 28). In the move from Chapelain’s outraged denunciation of no unity to Lot’s concerned if exaggerated imposition of perfect unity, we can chart a constant preoccupation with origins, an unspoken desire to validate the literary artifact by returning to its authorial source. !$ 12For a recent treatment of the phenomenon of interlace, see Micha, Essais, 94—1 22. 13}; is curious that Vinaver accepts Lot’s theory of unity for the Vulgate Cycle but finds it inapplicable to Malory. In Introduction The fact that Lot’s case for entrelacement and consistent chronology in the Prose Lancelot does not hold for other texts of the Vulgate Cycle weakens considerably his arguments for unity and single authorship. But even the calendar of interlaced events that so carefully maps the terrain of the Prose Lancelot gives us only part of the picture. It neglects the more elusive and certainly more problematic portions of the tales, those that stubbornly resist the confines of the literary-historical map. The task of accounting for these more anomalous but very prominent features of the Vulgate Cycle has fallen to scholars in the past fifteen years. Redirecting the illusory search for absent authors, origins, and textual unity, they have begun interrogating instead the complex relations between author and text as they appear on the pages of the lengthy prose cycle.!4 Accepting digression in narrative development, repetition of stock motifs, the plurality of authorial voices, self-contradiction, and ellipsis as givens of the prose romances, some recent studies embrace head-on the issues of narrative recasting and discontinuity as essential aspects of thirteenth-century prose composition. Examining linguistic fragmentation and interruption, analyzing the thematization of textual genealogy and paternity of literary characters, and invoking processes of intertextuality and rewriting, scholars have formulated new questions that set the prose romance squarely within the context of medieval manuscript transmission while underscoring simultaneously its theoretical modernity. Introduction the Romantic imagination at least—be vouchsafed by the signature of a verifiable historical author.15 THE UN-UNIFIED TEXT Standing behind current attempts to reformulate the problematic notions of authorship and textual coherence is an implicit recognition that the Old French prose romance, shrouded in the anonymity that so often accompanies literary works of the High Middle Ages in France, forms part of a manuscript tradition that allowed texts to be constantly recast and rewritten in many variants. Such works derive ultimately from the cumulative efforts of successive authors, scribes, and reader/reciters.!© The result in the case of the Vulgate Cycle is a corpus of five tales whose interdependence is both obvious and difficult to pinpoint. Taking as their subject the entire history of the Grail from its origin in the Passion of Christ to the successful accomplishment of the quest by the chosen hero, the prose texts adopt the comprehensive scale of literary and theological summae of the thirteenth century: Jean de Meun’s Roman de la Rose, Vincent de Beauvais’s Speculum Naturale, and Thomas Aquinas’s Summa Theologica. Like these structural analogues, the Vulgate’s summa arthuriana knots its component parts together in a relatively seamless whole. Potential boundaries separating the standard courtly narratives of love and chivalry found in the Lancelot, Mort Artu, and the Merlin from the Grail legends of the Queste and Estoire are skillfully obscured by an elaborate matrix of crossreferences that tie the whole together. The Lancelot announces at its beginning that Lancelot was given the baptismal name of Galahad, thus forging a crucial link between the archetypal knight-lover and the chosen hero of the Queste del Saint Graal. In the last third of the 15For a theoretical discussion of authorship that can be applied fruitfully to medieval texts, see Michel Foucault, “What Is an Author?” Textual Strategies, ed. XIX Lancelot, we learn that Lancelot is in fact Galahad’s father, having engendered the Grail hero during a visit to King Pelles’s daughter at Corbenic. The son far surpasses the more courtly Lancelot in spiritual achievement. Galahad represents the ideal conjunction of religious and chivalric modes, and of past and future epochs. Descending from King David on his father’s side and from Joseph of Arimathea and the Grail kings on his mother’s, he is the embodiment of Biblical history destined to cure the ills of the Arthurian world. His success at the task is ultimately undermined by events in the Mort Artu that lead inevitably to the downfall of King Arthur, the end of his realm, and the twilight of Arthurian chivalry previously established by Merlin’s creation of the Round Table. This concerted interweaving of individual narrative strains suggests that we should perhaps read all of the Vulgate tales together as a whole. But must we do so? And to what extent? Must we read the Mort Artu as deriving from and inextricably tied to the Queste Do we risk seriously misreading the Queste if we isolate it from later developments of the Mort? Alternatively, should we consider the Estoire or Merlin to be discrete textual entities, and can we justify reading the more lengthy Lancelot independently of its companion tales? A look at the extant manuscript tradition shows that neither option we have been discussing—whether taking the composite of all five tales as a textual whole or isolating individual tales as independent works—reflects medieval practice. Surviving manuscript evidence indicates that individual volumes of the cycle appeared only occasionally alone; they were accompanied more commonly by some or all of the companion tales, and in a surprising way. Grouping all five tales together was frequent but not the rule. Only nine out of some ninety-six _ surviving manuscripts contain the entire cycle. The corpus is most commonly sectioned into three groupings that regularly split apart one of what we would consider to be the cycle’s individual “texts”: the Lancelot. In the manuscript tradition as we now perceive it, the Estozre, the Merlin, and the continuation of the Vulgate Merlin (termed the Vulgate suite) most often fall xX together as one unit.!” The first two parts of the lengthy Prose Lancelot form another segment. And the last third of the Lancelot joins the Queste and Mort Artu in a final grouping. Of the extant manuscripts containing all or part of the Vulgate _romances, none offérs the entire Prose Lancelot ",intact.18 And the array of variation in textual presentation across the corpus is maximal. If the Queste appears at times alone, at times with the Lancelot and Mort Artu or alternately as part of a five-volume corpus as we have said, it also combines in some instances with the Lancelot alone, and in others with only the Mort. At least one manuscript joins the Estoire with the Queste and Mort.}9 These groupings suggest that a variety of possible readings were built into the highly flexible narrative structure of the long and rambling Vulgate tales and that textual boundaries as we know them actually varied from one reading/performance to the next. There is, then, no single definitive text of the Vulgate romances, and this not by oversight. Editors of Old French texts are well aware that the literary artifact in the High Middle Ages lies somewhere between the plurality of manuscript versions available to us on the one hand, and the lack of complete textual genealogy for any one tale on the other. If we are plagued by the loss of documentation through the years, by the absence of manuscript versions that could potentially tell us a good deal about the historical transmission of an individual text, we must also recognize that any text in the High Middle Ages was, in an important sense, fragmentary.?° This is perhaps best illustrated by the verse continuations of Chrétien de Troyes’s Perceval (1189-91). Within fifty years of the composition of Chrétien’s unfinished Grail romance, there appear four continuations: the Gawain Continuation and the Perceval Continuation both written before the end of the twelfth century, followed by Manessier and Gerbert de 174 discussion of the various Merlin texts is offered below. 18Alexandre Micha, ed. Lancelot: roman en prose du 13e siécle, vol. 1 (Geneva: Droz, 1980), ix—xxiii. 19 bert Pauphilet, ed. Two prologues to the cycle, the Elucidation and the Bliocadran, were composed subsequently. The process of narrative elaboration attested by these continuations constitutes an accumulation of materials that remain nonetheless fragmentary. From them we get a clear sense that the desire for a conclusion to the tale becomes an excuse for narrative amplification. No matter how many lines are added to Chrétien’s base text, they can never produce a single finished or unified work. And the problem is not simply that only a portion of the original manuscript corpus survives. For even if we had access to all the manuscripts that once existed for the Perceval material, or for any Old French text, we would not necessarily be better able to define the precise parameters of that text. Rather, we would be reminded all the more of the extent to which there was generally no definitive version of the medieval tale. This is the phenomenon of mouvance as Paul Zumthor has described it, a kind of textual variability that consistently undermines the authenticity of any Old French text.?! THE ELUSIVE AUTHOR As verifiable textual fixity recedes before our modern eyes, so too does the medieval writer’s potential authority. Indeed, recent work on Provengal lyric has shown that, for certain authors at least, the presumed existence of a single holograph of a particular poem is doubtful. It appears for example that Jaufré Rudel authored several distinct versions of a given poem, and that he did so not as an attempt to supplant an early version by a more accomplished or definitive successor, but simply as a means of expanding, elaborating, and diversifying the text at hand.?? We have no reason to believe that this process did not also inform the composition of Old French works, including texts in prose as well as in verse. In the case of the Vulgate Cycle, it is entirely possible that two interdependent phenomena served to blur the potential boundaries of a discrete text: the scribe could add sections to the text he copied, becoming in a sense 21 Essai de poétique médiévale (Paris: Seuil, 1972), 73. 22Rupert Pickens, The Songs of Jaufré Rudel (Toronto: The Pontifical Institute of Medieval Studies, 1978), 23. Introduction an author in his own right as he recast his model into an “original” version of the tale,2° and the author could redo his own work without clearly distinguishing the original from the rewrite.24 The Vulgate Cycle then provides us with a text that is not a text in the modern sense of the term, a text that is always fragmentary but always a composite of more than one text, a text located somewhere and uncertainly in the complex relation between many narrative versions created by many authorial if not authoritative hands. The literary map accurately representing this cycle of tales would contrast starkly with Lot’s set calendar. It would be a map that changed continually as we move through the narrative terrain it charts. Although it might incorporate on one level and for the text of the Prose Lancelot in particular the existence of a predictable calendar of events, a map detailing the whole of the Vulgate Cycle would have to reflect a much looser and more flexible narrative structure. It would be a map with no fixed perimeter, and no set or authorized format, a map that could shift and reshape itself at successive moments and with successive readings. This is precisely the kind of map that the Vulgate Cycle provides through its own overt references to textuality and authorship. Signaling us at every turn not to look for textual unity or single authorship among these pages, the cycle offers numerous literary signposts to guide our path in other directions. The clearest example is found in the elusive figure of the text’s putative author, a man whose actual role in the composition of the Vulgate Cycle remains as uncertain as the boundaries of the text he is reputed to have penned. This author’s name is itself a map: Walter Map. But in stark contrast to Lot’s calendar, this map does not deliver reassuring proof of an author’s controlling presence. 23Roger Dragonetti, La Vie de la lettre au Moyen Age (Paris: Seuil, 1980), 48. 24Fmmanuéle Baumgartner notes that by the end of the fourteenth century there existed five or six clearly distinct versions of the Prose Tristan: Version I, a short version that preceded the Vulgate Cycle; Version II, the longest and most popular; Version Il, a mix of versions I and II plus an interpolation of a fragment from the Prose Lancelot, Version IV, which combines Versions I, II, III and additional interpolations; and other interpolated versions. Le Tristan en Prose: Essai d’interprétation d'un roman médiéval (Geneva: Droz, 1975), 85-87. xx1 Credited with composing the Lancelot, Queste, and Mort, the historical Walter Map was a jurist and a man of letters at the court of King Henry II of England. An influential court figure, Map was also an author in his own right. Drawing on his experience as a canon and precentor, chancellor of Lincoln from 1186, and archdeacon of Oxford from 1197, Walter Map composed a satiric work about life at King Henry’s court called posthumously the Courtier’s Trifles (De Nugis Curialium). The epilogue to the Vulgate’s Queste casts Walter Map as an author in another capacity, making him responsible for transcribing official court records of Arthurian adventure from Latin into French. “When they had dined, King Arthur summoned his clerks who were keeping a record of all the adventures undergone by the knights of his household. When Bors had related to them the adventures of the Holy Grail as witnessed by himself, they were written down and the record kept in the library at Salisbury, whence Master Walter Map extracted them in order to make his book of the Holy Grail for the love of his lord King Henry, who had the story translated from Latin into French.”29 But Walter Map’s purported role in composing the Vulgate Cycle can be readily dismissed. He died in 1209, approximately five to ten years before the composition of the first tale that bears his name.2® Scholars have speculated that the anonymous authors of the Vulgate Cycle chose to append Map’s name to their fictive tales of knights and ladies in order to lend an air of historical veracity to the world of Arthurian wonder. Map’s association with Henry Il’s court was well established. And Henry enjoyed a legendary association with King Arthur. What better way to assert the historicity of Arthurian adventure than to make it flow from the pen of a master storyteller who had rubbed shoulders with the very king reputed to have launched the discovery of Arthur and Guenevere’s graves at Glastonbury? Yet even Map’s name as it appears in the Vulgate texts presents a curious anomaly. Some 25 Queste, ed. Pauphilet, 279-280. 26For extended discussions of the Vulgate Cycle’s dating, see F. Lot, Etude sur le Lancelot en prose, 126-140, and “Sur la date du Lancelot en prose,” Romania 57 (1931): 137-46, and J. Frappier, Etude sur La Mort le roi Artu, 20. xx12 think that “Walter Map” was a kind of joke, a nickname derived from the Welsh vab or mab or ap meaning “son of,” a tag used by the English to denote their Welsh friends on the border.27 In this case, the signature “Walter Map” that appears in the Vulgate Cycle would translate nonsensically as “Walter son of,” an unfinished epithet, a name that gives the illusion of identifying a historical author without doing so in fact. Repeated allusion to this name that does not really name reminds us pointedly that individual authorial contributions to the Vulgate Cycle are as difficult to discern as the boundaries separating one narrative “text” of the cycle from another. Map’s potential authority is diluted further by repeated reference to the textualized voice of li contes (“the story”) throughout the tales attributed to him. The epilogue citing Walter Map as the author of the Queste also cites li contes, a sort of inanimate narrative protagonist, as the official teller of the tale. The story ends not when Map stops speaking but when lL contes has nothing more to say about the Grail adventures, we are told. Map’s authoritative written record comes to us then only through a wholly fictive voice that speaks from the pages of Arthurian romance. If the authority we might attribute to the signature of this author is attenuated by the circumstances of his death and the uncertain status of his name, the potential force of his presence in the text is reduced all the more by the voice of i contes that accompanies and encloses it. The invocation of Walter Map as author of the Vulgate Cycle undermines the very purpose of citing an author as guarantor of a text’s worth. By taking us back to a reputed origin that it then withholds and obscures, this map turns us away from the empirical search for an original historical author and allied efforts to establish a coherent literary work where one clearly does not exist. And it is not the only signal guiding us in that direction. 27Walter Map, De Nugis Cunalium: Courtier's Trifles, ed. and trans. M.R. James, rev. C.N.L. Brooke and R.A.B. Introduction THE ESTOIRE DEL SAINT GRAAL AND THE MERLIN The titular author of the Estoire and the Merlin, one Robert de Boron, provides similarly suspect clues. Thought to have composed an early Grail story in verse, Joseph d’Arimathie (ca. 1200), Robert de Boron is also credited with subsequent prose elaborations of this tale known as the Roman du Graal (“Romance of the Grail”) and with their later development in the Vulgate texts. The Vulgate’s Estoive cites Robert as a scriptor who translated the tale we read from Latin into French, “et mesire Robers de Borom, qui ceste estoire translata de latin en francois.”28 The closing lines of the Merlin cite Robert de Boron as the teller of a tale derived from a book in the vernacular, the Livre dou Graal, “And I Robert de Boron who retell this book according to the teaching of the Livre dou Graal (“The Grail Book” ], it is fitting that I speak and recount the story just as the book tells it.”29 But Robert’s actual contribution to the composition of volumes of the Vulgate Cycle that bear his name remains as nebulous as the fictive genealogies advanced for these tales. If the Merlin were merely a copy of a single Grail story (Li Livres dou Graal), as the text states, it would not contain the deeds of Merlin and Arthur’s knights that it does in fact record. But how do these narrative strains come together? Merlin explains that the book he dictates to his scribe Blaise—an account of the reign of Uther and Pendragon—will be joined to the Grail story (“Joseph’s book”) when Blaise meets with the Grail people. But this crucial event in the development and transfer of the story we read never takes place. Merlin’s book predicts one set of events—Blaise passing on his narrative to the “gens du Graal” (“Grail followers”)—but narrates another—Merlin being seduced by Ninane and dying without ensuring that the book he wrote with Blaise’s help ever merged with a separate Grail narrative. Alongside the genealogy 28Eugéne Hucher, ed., Le Saint Graal (Le Mans: Monnoyer, 1875), 3:194, 269. Whereas Sommer’s edition provides a short version of the Estoire, Hucher’s text based on Cange MS. BNP 748 and Le Mans 354 offers a more elaborate narrative rendition. 29 Alexandre Micha, ed., Merlin: roman du XIIle siécle (Geneva: Droz, 1979), 290-291. Introduction that posits Robert de Boron as an author /translator of a text deriving from a mixture of an authoritative Grail book and pseudo-historical accounts of the Arthurian past, we find another genealogy establishing the fictive character Merlin as the only possible author for all the texts in question. If Merlin’s composite work remains distinct from the Livres dou Graal that Robert retells, then Robert’s exact contribution to the Merlin as we know it remains in doubt.?? We are left wondering how to reconcile the roles of two authors, Merlin and Robert de Boron, and how to weld together two fragments of a textual genealogy that do not fit together logically. The proposed genealogy for the Estoire is equally incomplete. This romance claims that its author, who figures as a character in the tale, transcribes a book that was previously written by Christ.3! As Christ hands the inscribed author a book containing the story of the Holy Grail, he directs him specifically to copy its contents, thereby guaranteeing the accuracy of the sacred text that becomes the Grail story we read (2:38). What then is the relation between Robert de Boron, the inscribed author, and the original creator, Christ? When Robert de Boron is said to have translated the estoire from Latin into French it appears that the estotre furnished the subject matter or source material for Robert’s French text. However, the term estoire is also used in this tale to refer to the current narration, Robert’s French translation as well as to the textualized voice that recounts it (3:269). The estoire is here said to tell the tale of the Grail story much as li contes does elsewhere in the cycle. This coupled with the fact the Robert’s text is called alternately the Estoire dou Saint Graal (3:269) and Li Contes dou Saint Graal (3:194) makes it impossible to establish a clear distinction between the Latin “source” and the subsequent French “translation.” Furthermore, it is unclear whether Robert de Boron, the purported translator of the Estoire, is to be identified with the author/narrator who appears in the tale. The trio formed by Robert, “I,” and the estoive is grounded in the same authorial ambiguity that characterizes the group of voices that recount the other Vulgate narratives: Map, li contes, and Arthur’s knights whose depositions are recorded by scribes and later retrieved by Walter Map to “make his book.” If the Vulgate’s textual genealogies demonstrate an obsession with origins that parallels that shared by Chapelain and Lot, they reveal simultaneously how, in the case of these narratives, the preoccupation with origins leads consistently to no verifiable authorial source. We are left rather with a plurality of authorial voices and competing subtexts that cannot be aligned in logical sequence. Credit for narrative invention falls on a cohort of fictive authors that range from the chivalric heroes who speak their adventures at King Arthur’s court to the fictive dictator Merlin and his vernacular scriptor Blaise, to the bogus author/translator Walter Map, the storyteller Robert de Boron, and the oracular voice of Christ. Amid all these references to creators and their sources, both written and oral, no mention is made, curiously, of the actual textual antecedents for the Vulgate Cycle. Yet there are many. The Vulgate Estoireis preceded historically by a prose Joseph attributed to Robert de Boron (alternatively called Le Grand Saint Graal), which derives in turn from Robert’s verse Joseph (Le Petit Saint Graal, Le Roman de L’Estoire du Graal). To this oldest known ancestor text for the Estoire are appended 504 extant verses of a fragmentary Merlin that remains unsigned. Different from subsequent reworkings for which there is a relatively rich extant manuscript tradition, these seminal texts in verse appear in a single manuscript edited by William Nitze as Le Roman de VEstoire dou Graal (Paris: Champion, 1927). As Robert’s original tales were recast into prose beginning around 1210, they emerged sometimes in a trilogy, Le Roman du Graal, that~\ recounts the history of the Grail vessel (Joseph d’Arimathie), its arrival in Great Britain along with the discovery of the future king Arthur (Merlin), the quest for the Holy Grail, and the subsequent demise of Arthur’s world (Perceval, known widely as the Didot Perceval). \ \ \ XXLU The assumption that Robert also penned a verse Perceval that served as a model for the later prose trilogies has recently been challenged. Of the fifteen surviving texts of the prose Joseph and fifty-five of the prose Merlin, only two Manuscripts contain the prose Perceval. These manuscripts are the best known because they have been edited: the Modena manuscript (E. 39 from the Bibl. Estense in Modena) edited most recently in its entirety by Bernard Cerquiglini and previously for the Joseph and Perceval segments only by William Roach.*? But it is highly probable that the texts of the prose Perceval, which do not bear Robert’s name, were composed from a combination of Chrétien de Troyes’s Perceval, the Second Continuation, and Robert’s Joseph and Merlin.*5 The verse Merlin too spawned serial prose rewrites. Having itself descended from Geoffrey of Monmouth’s Historia Regum Britanniae and Vita Merlini, passing into the French tradition through Wace’s Roman de Brut and other vernacular translations of Geoffrey’s Historia, the prose Merlin appears in fifty-five extant manuscripts, including Modena and Didot. It is recast again in the Vulgate Merlin and somewhat later in the Huth Merlin. The Modena Merlin represents the first stage of this elaborate prosification and offers the shortest version, devoid of a suite. The Vulgate Merlin expands Robert’s narrative by detailing Arthur’s military campaigns against rebellious barons in what is known as the Vulgate suzte; and the Huth Merlin (sometimes referred to as the Suite du Merlin) supplies a series of elaborate romance episodes. This rendition forms part of the post-Vulgate Roman du Graal (ca. 1230-40), formerly known as the pseudo—Robert de Boron Cycle, which is composed of a remodeled Vulgate Estoire, Queste, and Mort Artu, portions of the Vulgate Lancelot (taken from the “Agravain” section), segments 32Bernard Cerquiglini, ed., Le Roman du Graal: manuscrit de Modéne par Robert de Boron (Paris: Union Générale d’Edition, 1981); William Roach, ed., The Didot Perceval According to the Manuscripts of Modena and Paris (Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 1941); “The Text of the Modena Prose Joseph d’Arimathie,” Romance Philology 9 (1955-56): 313-342. 33Rupert Pickens, “Mais de ¢ou ne parole pas crestiens de troies...: A Re-examination of the Didot Perceval,” Romania 105 (1984): 492-510. Introduction from the prose Tristan (and the Suite du Merlin) .34 The compositional system charted here is one of extensive rewriting. The Vulgate Cycle expands the prose Perceval into two separate stories: the Queste del Saint Graal, which draws additional material from Chrétien de Troyes’s Conte du Graal and the Perceval Continuations, and the Mort Artu, which recasts source material from the chronicle tradition—Geoffrey of Monmouth’s Vita Merlini and Wace’s Roman de Brut—by adding the love story of Lancelot and Guenevere from Chrétien de Troyes’s Chevalier de la charrete (“The Knight of the Cart,” 1178-80). Unlike its predecessors, the Vulgate Cycle devotes a full half of its narrative to developing a lengthy rendition of Chrétien’s Lancelot story, perhaps using a predecessor of the Middle High German Lanzelet by Ulrich von Zatzikhoven (ca. 1200) to fill in details of the hero’s childhood. The prose Joseph and Merlin are similarly recast into the Estoire del Saint Graal and the Estoire de Merlin respectively. Rewriting of this material continues when authors of the Post-Vulgate Roman du Graal, the prose Tristan, and the Palamedes (late thirteenth century) pick up where the Vulgate authors left off. Not unique to the Vulgate material, the process of rewriting characterizes the majority of Old French texts. Most vernacular authors in the High Middle Ages based their writing on some preexisting materia in either Latin, French, or another language. Their texts also contain frequent comment on the very process of literary borrowing, explaining how their work either copies dutifully or diverges purposefully from its base text.35 Whereas the earliest French romancers build their narratives on Latin sources—on Statius’s Thebaid, Virgil’s Aeneid, an account of the Trojan War by pseudo-Dares and pseudo-Dictys, or various accounts of the life of Alexander the Great—Marie de France turns to Breton lais, explaining that she wants to recast them in French. Both Marie and authors of the French romances of antiquity see their literary 34¥For a detailed study of the Roman du Graal, see Fanni Bogdanow, The Romance of the Grail (Manchester: Manchester University Press, 1966). 35Douglas Kelly, “Theory of Composition in Medieval Narrative Poetry and Geoffrey of Vinsauf’s Poetria Nova,” Medieval Studies 31 (1969): 117-148. Introduction task as one of adapting a previous text, of transforming an existing narrative into something only partially new. This practice, which had the widest currency in the Middle Ages, effectively blurred potential distinctions between original and copy, author and impersonator. In the medieval system of rewriting, a reformulated text becomes to a degree the author’s own invention without ever really losing its former character. The literary work resides in a continuum of transformations, each different from but as valid as its predecessor. THE PROSE LANCELOT A particularly apt illustration of the process is provided by the Vulgate Lancelot The longest of the five Vulgate romances, the Lancelot alone accounts for half of the cycle, occupying three volumes of Sommer’s seven-volume edition. It is built around a central core supplied by Chrétien de Troyes’s Chevalier de la charrete. But Chrétien’s contribution to this narrative is thoroughly obscured; no clues indicate where his portion of the tale begins or ends. And rather than heading the narrative sequence, as is the case with Chrétien’s Perceval in the verse continuations, the Charrete is embedded in the middle of a narrative scenario that radiates out from it.%6 The “Galehaut” portion of the prose text— which includes the reworking of Chrétien’s tale—appears in volume 3 of Sommer’s edition, the “Suite de la Charrete” in volume 4, and the “Agravain” in volume 5.37 In elaborating Chrétien’s 7,126 lines of verse into roughly 2,500 pages of prose, the Vulgate Lancelot does not simply add new narrative material to its base text. Certain key scenes in the Charrete—the mounting of the cart and the tournament at Pomeglai for example—are actually reduced in the prose version, while details are provided to flesh out other scenes left enigmatic and vague in Chrétien’s text. The prose romancer tells us how Kay and Lancelot 36For a detailed discussion of narrative elaboration in the Prose Lancelot see Bruckner on “Intertextuality.” 37Alexandre Micha’s edition begins in medtas res so that to read the Lancelot story chronologically in this edition one must begin with volumes 7 and 8 and then proceed to volumes 1 through 6. XxXU meet, under what circumstances Kay and Meleagant fight together, and how Lancelot and Meleagant do battle on two occasions, thereby providing answers to questions that Chrétien’s richly ambiguous text leaves open. In the prose Lancelot, scenes are often displaced from their original narrative sequence and expanded through a process of doubling: the cart episode repeats with Bors and other knights stepping aboard after Lancelot’s fateful move and the cemetery scene features two tombstones necessitating two tests for the initiate knight.*8 But even this thorough absorption of Chrétien’s text into the Vulgate’s narrative does not create a clearly unified whole. The prose redaction seems to have existed in at least two major narrative versions. Although the Vulgate —\ | | Lancelot is generally called the Prose Lancelot, one must distinguish between the Vulgate version of the tale and the noncyclic Prose Lancelot, a shorter version designed possibly to stand independently of the Queste and the Mort Artu.*° Both cyclic and noncyclic Lancelos recount the hero’s childhood, education, and knightly adventures up to his installation as a knight of the Round Table. The shorter version then offers a brief account of the journey to Sorelois and False Guenevere episodes with no narrative bridge to the Queste and Mort Artu. The longer, cyclic version elaborates those same episodes to prepare the reader for the Grail material that will follow in subsequent texts. The two prose Lancelots thus reflect two stages of narrative development within the prose rewrite itself: the first stage exalting earthly love and chivalry between Lancelot and the queen, the second casting those very practices as highly problematic and dangerous. Certainly one of the major shifts as we move from courtly romance of the twelfth century to the cyclic Grail material of the thirteenth is the shift from a secular quest for the Arthurian lady to the spiritual search for the venerated if mysterious Grail object. In the Prose Lancelot, Lancelot’s interest in the queen appears at times to be more political than personal. If he is attracted to Galehaut emotionally, and perhaps sexually, he favors Guenevere as a conduit to another powerful man, the king. When Chrétien’s phrasing about mutual love and enjoyment between Lancelot and the queen is replaced by a discourse of explicit seduction between Lancelot and Galehaut, the classic configuration of courtly love takes on a new dimension. As Galehaut transforms his original plot to steal Guenevere from Arthur into a plan of capturing Lancelot’s love and attention, he invokes the standard discourse of courtly love to express undying affection for another knight, not a lady: “It would be worth having my great honor turned to shame, if I could be as sure of him [Lancelot] as I would wish him to be of me.™4 The apparently passionate and abiding union that links Lancelot to Guenevere is here shown to be fraught with substantial dissonance and disunion. If rewriting the tale of Lancelot and Guenevere has made it longer, fuller, and more abundant in words, it has also explored the cracks between these amplified segments of narrative. That we have more of a story does not mean that we have more synthesis, resolution, or controlled structure. In fact, the opposite is true. The protracted process of recasting and elaborating fragments of preexisting literary texts that generates the Vulgate Cycle as we know it creates a narrative that spreads in many contradictory directions across the manuscript page. To chart this spread accurately, we would need a literary map devoid of clear directional bearings. From the former vantage point, images are distorted, accuracy is accompanied by exaggeration, directional control gives way to flux. The three-dimensional whole, while still composed of the sum of its parts, no longer possesses the artificially imposed completeness of its twodimensional representation, though it claims to do just that. THE WHOLE AND ITS PARTS It is this anomalous condition of fragmentation posing as wholeness that some recent studies have attempted in different ways to capture. Linguistic analyses have shown how the very prose style of the Vulgate romances creates a vision composed of many isolated and atomized details, suggesting that the story we read is more realistic than its enigmatic twelfth-century precursors. Yet the numerous indications of time and place in the Prose Lancelot, for example, form part of a succession of fixed images that resist any final comprehensive synthesis. The Vulgate’s abundance of precise detail does not contribute in the end to a fuller or more realistic picture of the whole.*® Similarly, repeated reference to the speech act, which would seem to prioritize the communicative role of speech in the prose Joseph, actually calls attention to the ephemeral or questionable status of speech in the prose setting. The uninterrupted flow of direct discourse between interlocutors that characterizes the earlier verse composition of Robert de Boron is replaced in the prose rewrite by a constant, rhythmic reference to the fact that the speakers are speaking. Direct address is typically prefaced by remarks to the effect that “this person now speaks,” or “that one now responds.” And the stream of narrative events in twelfth-century romance, often punctuated by direct authorial intervention, is here replaced by repeated allusion to the textualized voice of 45Qn the distinctive way that certain prose narratives emphasize their material character, see Michele Perret, “De espace romanesque 4 la matérialité du livre,” Poétique 50 (April 1982): 17-37. 46 Baumgartner, “Les Techniques narratives,” 186. XXUI1 contes as the principal teller of the tale we read. When we hear constantly that “the tale tells us...,”° “the tale speaks...,” or “the tale now turns from one hero to recount the deeds of another”—a rhetorical technique used widely in the Vulgate narratives themselves—the predominance of the narrator’s “I” is significantly diluted and diffused.4” In both cases, the illusion of full-bodied and unmediated speech—generated either between literary characters or between author and audience—is fractured by incessant reminders of the textual, written medium that records that seemingly plentiful voice. The chronology of the Vulgate romances reinforces this sensation of nonlinear time, returning us constantly to sources and origins of characters and the narratives they inhabit only to reveal all too cogently that those origins are irretrievable and artificially constructed.48 As a text written late in the development of the Vulgate Cycle but positioned near the head of the literary series, the Merlin offers a richly atemporal view toward past and future narrative events. While exploiting factual antecedents already related in the Lancelot it announces them as events to be recounted subsequently. The text stands in the Vulgate corpus as a predecessor of the Lancelot-Grail trilogy but a predecessor curiously cognizant of its own future development. The apparent linear sequence we follow from the Estozre to the Merlin, Lancelot, Queste, and Mort Artu is actually predicated on a narrative circularity that allows later texts to influence their seeming precursors. The elaborate genealogical trees attesting to the sources and origins of individual characters in the corpus are structured similarly so as to turn in circles. In the Merlin, Sagremor the Unruly offers an especially cogent illustration of the instability of paternal relations. His incestuous origins label him alternatively as the son, the grandson, or the nephew of the emperor of Constantinople. The incompleteness of Sagremor’s lineage, like that of Galahad and so many other protagonists in the Vulgate Cycle, goes hand in hand with the discontinuous romance narrative. It has in fact been suggested that the very objective of the Huth Merlin is to reveal how paternity—whether that of the son owing his existence to his father or that of the literary text dependent on a textual origin—validates the potential importance of origins while also undercutting their absolute worth.5° For all its talk of origins and sources, when emphasizing the details of a character’s identity or history, the source of a speaker’s voice, a text’s words, or a character’s lineage, the Vulgate Cycle demonstrates vividly how those sources are necessarily superseded by elements in the narrative that hark back to them: the text we read then becomes both an image or representation of its purported sources and a renun- { ciation of them. One is led by these false ge- nealogical clues to wonder why the Vulgate Cycle insists so actively on spurious, fictive origins, obscuring all the while its actual debt to tangible literary sources. Why do these tales evoke the names of Walter Map and his archival record, Robert de Boron and his livre, the oral deposition of Arthur’s knights, Merlin’s oral dictation to Blaise, Christ’s instructive and creative word, while never mentioning Chrétien de Troyes or Geoffrey of Monmouth? Of course, the invocation of false authors and fake textual genealogies was common practice in medieval text production generally. Geoffrey, of Monmouth himself claims, in the Historia Regum Britanniae, to be translating a Breton text given to him by one Walter, archdeacon of Oxford. Layamon purports to have derived his Brut from an unattested text by Augustine and Albin. Much later, Chaucer cites as his source for Troilus and Criseyde a Latin author Lollius instead of crediting Boccaccio. Introduction when he has no authoritative source to validate his remarks. But the Vulgate Cycle’s particular version of this pervasive medieval tendency to cite invented sources can perhaps best be understood in relation to the complex shift from verse to prose that shaped the evolution of Arthurian romance from the twelfth to the thirteenth century. VERSE AND PROSE Just why prose emerged around 1210 as a viable medium in the writing of Arthurian romance is not yet fully understood. But this crucial stage in the development of Old French narrative calls up questions of oral versus written delivery, fantasy versus truth telling, fictive elaboration versus historical documentation. These fundamental questions address the very role and function of vernacular textuality in the High Middle Ages and raise in yet another way the question of origins. Prior to the thirteenth century, vernacular prose, like its Latin counterpart, had been reserved largely for recording legal and religious truths. It appeared in juridical texts, charters, religious writings, translations of the Bible, and sermons. Prose was used in the thirteenth century to document historical events in the chronicles of Villehardouin, Robert de Clari, Henri de Valenciennes, and, in the fourteenth century, the Histoire de Saint Louis by Joinville. But obviously fictive tales of Arthurian knights that were probably delivered orally to a listening public had previously appeared only in verse. As prose became an acceptable means of telling stories of love and adventure in the early thirteenth century, the polarity between orally delivered vernacular tales and more erudite writings in Latin began to collapse. The scope of the courtly narrative became simultaneously more historical and more religious, as the Vulgate Cycle readily attests. The newly cast prose romances began to incorporate within their narrative structure frequent claims to authenticity and veracity de signed, it would seem, to obscure their fictive origins. The closing lines of the Mort Artu present Walter Map as the author of an accurate and truthful written document: “And now Walter Map has no more to say about the Story of Lancelot, because he has brought it to an end Introduction and told everything that happened; his book ends here, and anything else that might be added would be a lie.”! This assertion combined with the allusion to Walter Map’s task as author/translator of the Queste discussed above reflects a mode of composition that mimics the writing of chronicle. Purporting to offer a truthful, authoritative record of past events, the system outlined in the Queste and Mort Artu moves from an eyewitness oral account of what are posited as actual events—the adventures of Arthur’s knights—to a recording of those events in writing, and a subsequent retrieval and translation of the archival document. The Estozre evokes a different avenue to establishing a truthful narrative: by capturing words from the mouth of the divine Creator, setting them down in writing and producing exact copies that preserve their valued essence. The veracity of the final text, here obviously a product of a nonsacred and vernacular tradition of storytelling, is guaranteed by repeated allusion ‘to the tale being true, as true as Scripture, as accurate as the apostles’ tales (2:388, 428, 439). If these textual genealogies attest to an overwhelming desire to legitimate the fanciful Arthurian stories of knights and ladies by anchoring them in the apparent accuracy of historical chronicle or the acclaimed Truth of Scripture, they reveal at the same time how vernacular romance is incapable of both tasks. God and King Arthur are equally removed from the realia of thirteenth-century existence. It is as difficult to represent the transcendental signified in tales of adventure as to revive the historical past in Arthurian prose. What the Vulgate tales offer as an alternative is the fictional creation of both God and Arthur ex nihilo, a kind of representation that does not depend on the meaningful Truth of Scripture or the truth of historical document, but on fictional intertexts that are more present and “real” than God or Arthur could ever be. It is these intertexts that structure the cycle’s elaborate textual genealogies. For Arthur’s knights, the antecedent story that guides the creation of their tales lies in those episodes previously recounted at King Arthur’s court. They seek pointedly for adventures that are “worth telling,” adventures that re- 51a Mort le roi Artu, ed. Jean Frappier (Geneva: Droz, 1964), 263. XXX semble as closely as possible those feats of heroism already undertaken, told aloud and written down at Arthur’s court. The source of their oral narrative could not be more literary. For Walter Map, the privileged intertext is found in the written record of chivalric deeds housed in the archive at Salisbury, an invented record deriving ostensibly from those same oral accounts that draw in turn on the Arthurian adventure story. Blaise composes his text from the dictation of a fictive character Merlin, and Robert de Boron draws on a “Livres dou Graal” that cannot be traced to any verifiable source. The Estoire's author rewrites a story that has been written previously by Christ; we read a secularized, chivalric version of a tale transformed. In all cases, the supposed copy of an original source proves to be an original text itself, a wholly literary text whose claims to greater authority both mask and reveal its implicit project. What we hear in the Vulgate Cycle’s claims to possessing the authority of chronicle or the truth of Scripture is not an evocation of actual sources, but a subtle appropriation into the literary sphere of the legitimacy that those sources traditionally provide. While stating so emphatically that their narratives derive from historical and scriptural sources, the Vulgate romances say at the same time: these are wholly literary texts, as accurate as history, as true as Scripture, as legitimate as any truthtelling narrative. But the truth told here is obviously of a different sort. It is a truth not of events or revelations, but a truth anchored solidly in the pleasurable, rhetorical use of words.>? Herein lies the answer to critical objections raised by Chapelain and Lot. For the insistent repetition of too many words that put Chapelain to sleep and offended the aesthetic sensibilities of Ferdinand Lot lies at the very heart of the Vulgate’s project to validate the literary text over and above its more erudite predecessors. Repetition serves in many ways as the hallmark of the Vulgate romances: repetition of authorial voices, of stock motifs and thematic material, or of whole segments of narrative lifted from the Queste and relocated in the Estoire. And that repetition draws attention to the specifically literary character of the Vulgate romances, undermining their professed pretentions to more lofty theological or historical expression. 52Burns, Arthurian Fictions, chap. 1. XXX In the Neoplatonic Christian tradition of the Middle Ages, repetition is conceived of primarily in a Vertical dimension; repetition of an event is a further concretization of the abstract Idea or Christian Ideal that precedes it.54 In transposing repetition to a horizontal plane, the Vulgate romances recast the process of theological representation into a literary system of intertextual rewriting and narrative reprise In Augustinian terms, this would constitute an overt and extreme case of textual idolatry, since preference is given clearly to the letter not the spirit, to the proliferation of words at the expense of the Word of God.54 The Vulgate Cycle cultivates, above all else, the seductive verbal trap that the Church Fathers warned against. Augustine’s denunciation of literature as fables, falsehoods, and lies that delight men instead of leading them beyond the text to the Word, may have been taken to heart by believers like St. Peter Damian, who during the eleventh century took Christ as his “literature.”°> But the medieval lay audience was apparently harder to convince. Thirteenth-century clerical pronouncements deplore the falsehoods and lies written about Perceval and the Holy Grail, lamenting those who have abandoned religious truth in preference for stories about Lancelot and the secularized holy relic. If the Grail material is the most religious component of the Vulgate corpus, it appeared as most irreligious to medieval Church authorities. LA QUESTE DEL SAINT GRAAL Of all the Vulgate romances, the Queste del ‘Saint Graal goes the farthest in attempting to mask the literariness of vernacular romance by imposing upon it a grid of religious interpretation. Does this mean that the vernacular adventure story has successfully escaped the limitations of earthly speech and narrative fabrication, acceding to the status of a religious tract, as Albert Pauphilet thought?56 Or should we more accurately read this narrative as a romance text whose Arthurian paternity has traditionally been denied by an _ overly Christianized interpretation?>’? When we look closely at exactly what is altered by the hermits’ presence in the Queste, we can see how this most religious of the Vulgate narratives joins its companion tales in cultivating the horizontal repetition of rewriting rather than offering a vertical representation of transcendent meaning. Although the hermits are asked typically to pro vide the vérité or truth of a preceding adventure or to relate the senefiance or meaning of chivalric exploits, they most often simply recast the initial event in another narrative register, evoking a parallel tale from the Biblical or chivalric past. Rather than providing interpretive glosses in abstract language, the hermits’ pronouncements tend to disperse the core of the adventure story into a series of intertexts, which, like the plural authorial voices in the Estoireand the Merlin, result in an anomalous combination of proliferation and repetition.5® Meaning in the Queste is not first hidden and then revealed, but rather it is systematically displaced from one textual segment to the next.59 In recasting tales from Scripture into the vernacular and placing them squarely within the world of Arthurian adventure, the hermits’ remarks subtly collapse the crucial distinction between sacred and secular narrative, legitimizing the vernacular enterprise under the guise of al- 564.
