Introduction legory. If the hermit here poses as the official and final voice of Arthurian romance, the influence his fictive presence exerts on the composition of the vernacular tale is no more religious than Walter Map’s participation in that same enterprise is historical. LA MORT ARTU The most chronicle-like of the Vulgate narratives is perhaps the Mort Artu, which exhibits less of the repetition so common in the other Vulgate tales.°° But the Mort Artu effects a narrative sleight of hand analogous to that of the Queste, allowing in the end for the most fundamental narrative repetition of all. Evoking the finality of historical events and the chronicles that record them as a model of narrative composition, this last volume of the Vulgate Cycle announces at the same time how, despite these pretensions, its own narrative remains essentially ahistorical. Offering a chilling and brutal finale to the seemingly interminable tales of adventure that precede it, the Mort Artu lays out an inexorable chain of cause and consequence in which the continued love affair between Lancelot and Guenevere rekindles a clan vendetta between Arthur’s family and Lancelot’s that eventually draws the king away from his kingdom and makes his bastard son Mordred’s treason possible. A final battle on Salisbury Plain, where King Arthur and Mordred kill each other, brings the cycle to a definitive close. As the Arthurian family line dies out, romance adventures come to an abrupt end. With the seeming precision of historical documentation, this tale records the end of an era. Or so it seems. When King Arthur dies, his grave is marked by a tombstone proclaiming his might and fame: “Here Lies King Arthur Who by His Valor Conquered Twelve Kingdoms” (La Mort Artu, 251). Prior to assuming this final resting place, however, Arthur is seen striding gallantly aboard a fairy ship, his horse and armor in tow, as if to continue his chivalric deeds forever in another 60For a detailed analysis of the compositional processes at work in this text, see Jean Rychner, L’articulation des phrases narratives dans “La Mort le roi Artu” (Geneva: Droz, 1970). On the “linear perspective “ of the Mort Artu, see Norris J. Lacy, “Spatial Form in the Mort Artu,” Symposium 31,4 (1977): 341, 343. XXX land. The finality of the words inscribed on Arthur’s tombstone are thus undermined by the enduring possibility that the legendary king may indeed return. This miraculous gesture implies that the story is not yet over and that the romance tradition has not yet died. The very moment of literary closure is here cast in a mode of open-endedness that puts the status of inscription in doubt. We see elsewhere in the Mort Artu how Arthur’s court writes its history on the tombstones of knights that lie in cemeteries, the inscriptions appearing to stand as a durable testament to events that took place. But it is revealed in certain cases that these funerary inscriptions are not wholly accurate.®* And as their status is called into question, so too the status of that other inscription—the writing down of Arthurian adventure from the knights’ oral deposition—loses even more of its potential authoritative force. When read against the tenuous finality of Arthur’s tombstone, the Mort Artu’s claim to truthful finality sounds a hollow note. If the text’s bold contention that Walter Map here provides a complete and accurate record of everything that actually happened to King Arthur’s knights lends an air of historical veracity to the Vulgate tales, it exposes at the same time the fallibility of Arthurian claims to historical accuracy. Recent studies of the Vulgate Cycle have made two things especially clear. They explain, if without meaning to do so, the compulsion of so many earlier scholars to discern systems of coherence in the Vulgate corpus. They demonstrate, in an unexpected way, how early arguments for narrative unity or authorial control were not conditioned by the critical predilections of their practitioners alone. Current work has amply revealed how the Vulgate corpus issues a host of false clues to the unsuspecting reader. Mention of named authors, allusion to authoritative textual paternity, a concerted emphasis on the genealogy of characters, claims to possess the historical veracity of an eyewitness account, alignment with authoritative Biblical predecessors, and invocation of meaningful 6lLeupin, Le Graal et la littérature, chap. 6. 62Helen Solterer, “‘Conter le terme de cest brief’: linscription dans La Mort le roi Artu,” Actes du 14e congrés international arthurien (Rennes: Presses Universitaires de Rennes, 1984), 558-568. XXXII prophecy all lend an air of accuracy and believability to these otherwise obviously fictive tales. But these leads, often embraced unquestioningly by scholars who find in them comfortable echoes of their own critical predilections, do not reflect the whole narrative picture. Indications of authorship and authoritative origins are countered at every turn in the complex and richly varied prose texts by narrative strategies that undermine and question the very possibility that narrative coherence and authorial mastery might prevail in a literary text. On the strictly material level, elaborate narrative repetition, interruption, and fragmentation undermine the wholeness of purported textual genealogies, or characters’ established paternity. These ruptures lead to larger but related questions that the Vulgate narratives invite us to pursue. What does it mean when obviously fictive tales call their fabrication true? When they create false signatures, sources, and origins for themselves? Or claim to possess the historical truth of chronicle or the sacred truth of Scripture? How does the function of authorship change along with the passage from verse to prose at the turn of the thirteenth century? What happens when secular romance poses as allegory (as it does in the Queste)? Or as chronicle, as in the Mort Artu? And what becomes of courtly love that provided the mainstay of twelfth-century romance? These are some areas of inquiry that the Vulgate Cycle explores, not in a predictable way that could be charted on a definitive map but by wandering across the uneven and evocative terrain of Arthurian romance. In their narrative wandering, the thirteenthcentury prose tales of love and adventure remind us that when analyzing them we need not look for a reassuring map to guide our literary voyage. And that in taking this trip we need not choose necessarily between unity and disunity, coherence and incoherence, between the ingenious author’s masterpiece and the barbarian’s literary dungheap. These excessively polarized options are perforce limiting and exclusionary in their own way. Possessing all the apparent fullness of a Mercator map, they necessarily distort the world they represent. But that very distortion can lead us to ask more productive questions, in particular questions about those sectors of the literary terrain that the quest for authority Introduction and textual unity has so often marginalized or effaced. The one who, by order of the Great Master, is setting* in writing the high and noble story of the Grail first sends greetings to all those men and women [II: 2]3 who believe in the glorious Holy Trinity, that is, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit—the Father, who creates [3] and gives life to all things; the Son, who [4] delivers all those who believe in Him from perpetual pain and brings them to the high joy without end; the Holy Spirit, who sanctifies and purifies good things. The name of the writer of this story is not divulged at the beginning. However, the words that will be said herein will permit you to know a great deal about his name,’ his life, and his ancestry. But he does not wish to reveal his name at the beginning, for three reasons. First, if he gave his name and said that through him God had revealed such a noble and lofty story as that of the Grail, the foundation of all stories, the treacherous and envious might interpret it as boastfulness. The second reason is that someone who knows him might hear his name, and thus might prize the story less, because it had been written down by such a humble person—for he holds himself to be the most humble and despised person ever created. The third reason is that if there were anything improper in the story, through either the omissions or the [5] naiveté of writers who later transmit it from one place to another, all the blame would be placed on him. For there are now in our times more mouths that recount evil than good,> and a man? is blamed more for doing a single bad deed than he is praised for one hundred good ones. For these three reasons he does not wish his name to be completely revealed, even though no matter how much he may wish to cover it up and hide it, it will be better known’ than he would like. However, he will clearly reveal how the high history of the Holy Grail was confided to him and when, and who gave it to him. 1 Corresponds to Hucher II: 1-39; Sommer I: 1-12; Ponceau §1-15. On all the other days, the Sacrament is celebrated as a sign that He was sacrificed for us, but on the day that He was truly crucified—this day, Good Friday—it is not, for there is no sign, since the day has come when He was truly crucified. Then he said to me, “Now [22] I will put you whence I took you, and then you will receive your Savior more certainly than you did before, for you should not receive a guest you do not know. And if you have seen great marvels, you will find some in this little book that you will not hold to be any less marvelous; but you will not look at it again before you have celebrated the Resurrection of Jesus Christ your Savior.” Thereupon, he put my spirit back in my body, and I felt just like someone who has slept and who awakens; and I thought I would see the angel, but he had gone. I looked and saw my Savior—the Eucharist—before me as it was when the angel carried me away; I took it, received it, and took communion with good will and great devotion. When the service was over, I took the little book and placed it in a small chest where the box containing the host was kept. After that I locked the chest tightly with a key, as I wanted” to protect it, and I knew no better place to put it, for it was a very beautiful and pure spot. When I left the chapel, I saw that it was already so late [23] that it was getting dark; I entered my little house and ate such food as Our Lord had given me. Thus I spent this day and the next, until the day of the Resurrection of the Savior came. And when it pleased Him that I perform the service of the day, which is as holy as Our Savior, who sanctified the day, I entered with certainty and ran immediately to the book to see the holy words, for they were so sweet and pleasant to hear that they made me forget all the hunger of the body. When the child came of age to marry, his relatives exhorted him to do so, but he was so in love with Jesus Christ because of his mother’s guidance that he said he would never marty any other but Holy Church, for he believed in God and had been baptized by the hand of Saint James the Minor, who was bishop of Jerusalem for a long time after Jesus Christ’s death. Joseph remained in prison, as you have heard, until forty-two years had passed. And then Vespasian, the emperor of Rome, freed him, and you will hear how this came about. Joseph was in prison for forty-two years without ever leaving, nor was he ever given anything other to eat than bread and water, and very little of that, about every three days. On the day that Jesus Christ was crucified, [73] Tiberius Caesar was emperor of Rome, and he remained in power for ten more years. Afterwards reigned his nephew Gaius, who lived [74] only one year. And then Claudius ruled the Roman empire for fourteen years; then Nero [75] who held the empire fourteen®* years. Following Nero came Titus and his son,2° Vespasian, who was ill. In the [76] third year of Titus’s reign,24 Joseph was freed from prison. This is indeed forty-two years, counting from the [77] Crucifixion of Our Lord Jesus Christ up to Joseph’s liberation, and you will hear how he was freed. Il 3. Vespasian Is Healed; Joseph of Arimathea Is Liberated. The first year Titus was emperor, it happened that his son Vespasian became so ill with leprosy that no one could go near him. This distressed Titus so much that he could not be comforted. And so he caused it to be known throughout all the lands that the one who could cure his son of leprosy would have whatever gift he might request. Though the emperor had made this known everywhere, he found no one who could cure his son until it happened that a knight who came to Rome from Capernaum heard about it. When he came before the emperor, he said he would willingly speak to his son for his benefit. The emperor had him taken to a window of a room where Vespasian was all alone. It was through this window that they spoke to him, for otherwise they could not bear the stench coming from him. After Vespasian had put his head out the window, the knight looked at him and saw that he was sicker than anyone could imagine. Vespasian asked at once if he knew of anything that could help him. And the knight answered, “My lord, certainly, I came to see you because I once had leprosy in my childhood.” “Oh, dear sir,” said Vespasian, “how were you cured of it?” “Indeed,” said he, “by a Prophet who was in Judea, whom the Jews wrongly killed.” “How did he cure you of it?” asked Vespasian. “Truly,” he replied, “all He did was touch me, and at once I was completely cured.” “What!” said he. “Was he so powerful that he cured leprosy?” “Indeed, my lord,” said the knight, “He did even more, for He raised the dead.” And he asked why he had been killed. “Certainly, my lord,” said the knight, “because He preached the truth and reproached the Jews for their wickedness. And I believe that if you had something He had touched, you would be immediately cured.” When the young man heard this, he was overjoyed. He sent for his father and had this told to him, for he could barely speak. And Titus said he would send a messenger to see if something could be found that He had touched. “My lord,” said Vespasian, “ask this knight to go, since he is from the land, and give him whatever riches he needs to take this message, for my heart tells me I will be cured. And if I can be healed, I promise the Prophet to take vengeance for the shameful thing the Jews did to Him.” Titus implored the knight until he said he would take his message. After that, he looked in a mirror to see if he recognized himself. When Vespasian saw him, he said, “My lord, be happy, for I know truly that I will be healed.” And then he told him his dream. At these words, the knight arrived. He prepared his baggage at once and set out to go to Judea, taking the knight with him. And he made him lord of all his household. The History of the Holy Grail When Joseph’s wife heard this news, she and her son came before him. She asked for justice for her lord, whom they had taken from her, and whom she had had no sign of since. He asked her why they had done this. The lady said, “Because he removed Jesus from the cross and put Him in his sepulcher.” Upon hearing this, he swore that he would burn them all if they did not tell him where Joseph was. They replied that he could burn them, for they could not return him, nor did they know what had become of him. And they were telling the truth, for they did not know what had really happened. Of the two who had put him in prison, only one was alive, for the other one had been beheaded within a week after imprisoning Joseph. And the jailer had fallen from the windows of the tower to the ground the day after they stopped giving Joseph food. Therefore, only one person was still alive; this was Caiaphas, who was the bishop of the Jews the year that Jesus Christ died.4 When they saw that all of them were to die, they said he could do as he wished with them, for it was true that they had seized Joseph, but they had handed him over to two of their number because they did not want everyone to know where he was imprisoned. Caiaphas was one of these two;° if he knew nothing, no one could ever give Vespasian any news. So Vespasian asked to see Caiaphas; once he had come before him, he had him well guarded while all the others were burned. After they were [112] burned, he told Caiaphas he would punish him more severely than any man had ever been if he did not return Joseph. Caiaphas answered that he could punish him in whatever way he pleased, for even if all the men in the world had sworn to return Joseph alive, they® could not, unless God Himself were to do so. But he would show him where Joseph had been imprisoned, for he did not know whether he was still alive. Vespasian said that he asked for nothing better. And Caiaphas said that he would do so, provided that he not be slain or burned. Vespasian assured him of this, promising that he would not have him killed by fire or sword. Then Caiaphas took him to the tower where the pillar was and said, “My lord, he was put in this pillar right after Jesus was crucified, and I was not yet thirty-three’ years old, who now am aged, as you can see.” Vespasian said to him, “Do not be afraid; the One for whom he was imprisoned there is powerful enough to keep him safe and sound, and even more, for He healed me, who had never served Him, from the most vile disease that ever was.” Vespasian then ordered Caiaphas to enter the jail, and if he did not find Joseph alive, to bring out the bones. Caiaphas said he would not go in, even if he were threatened with dismemberment. Therefore he did not realize that so much time had passed, nor did he think the emperor would have changed in such a short time, for the light Jesus Christ brought him when He appeared had never failed; so he thought nightfall had never come. Vespasian called Joseph and the members of his household and asked what he should do about Caiaphas, without breaking his promise [117] neither to slay nor to burn him. There were those who judged that he should be put in the prison where Joseph had been, so that he would die of hunger there. If he had him drowned, he would be killed neither by sword or fire. Joseph said, “My lord, you have the power and the authority to do this, but for God’s sake do not act in this way, for perhaps he will yet change his ways and believe in the One who kept me safe and sound for so long and delivered me from his hands and those of my other enemies. Perchance Our Lord will be served so well that He would not want him to die at this time.” Vespasian replied, “Since this is what you wish, I will take your advice, and I will not bring about his death; but I must take vengeance in some way for the death of the Lord, whom he wrongly caused to die. After all the people had prayed before the ark, they left the wood and set out on their way, traveling until they arrived at a city called Sarras, between Babylon? and Salamander. From this city came the first Saracens. Those who say that the Saracens are named after Abraham’s first wife are not to be believed, for this was falsely invented, nor does it seem reasonable. It is not unknown that Sarah was a Jew, and her son Isaac was a Jew, as were all those who were Isaac’s issue. Because the greatest part is considered to represent the whole, and since Jews descended from Sarah, it does not seem reasonable that the Saracens took their name from her. But they were called Saracens after this city named Sarras, because this was the first city where they became certain of what they worshiped. And in this city was founded and established the [129] sect that the Saracens maintained until the coming of Mohammed, who was sent to save them, though he damned himself first, and them afterwards, by his gluttony. Before the founding of the sect, the people of Sarras had no faith, but worshiped everything that pleased them, so that what they worshiped one day was not worshiped the next. But then they established the worship of the sun and the moon and the other planets. On the eleventh day after leaving Jerusalem, Joseph came to this city with his followers. Upon their arrival at the city’s entrance, Our Lord called him and said, “Joseph, you shall go into the city and preach My name, and baptize all those who receive the faith, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.” Joseph then replied, “Lord, how will I know how to preach so well, I who have never undertaken such a thing?” And Our Lord said to him, “Fear not about this, for you have only to open your mouth, and IJ will put into it a great abundance of words. Nor will you ever find any man, no matter how valiant or learned, who can resist the words I *Babylon is the name by which Cairo was generally known during the Middle Ages. 16 will deliver from your mouth. And I will make you like My apostles, through [130] the miracles and prodigies that I will perform through your hands. But take care that your faith does not become cold, for as long as you are a true believer, anything you dare to ask for will be granted in your need. Now go and think about doing my work, so that you may be paid as a loyal servant. And whatever menace you may receive, be not afraid, for I will watch over you and defend you, wherever you may go.” Joseph left at once and entered the city with his followers. When the inhabitants of the city saw so many people together—for they numbered at least seventy-five— and saw that they were barefoot, they began to wonder who these people were. Joseph and his disciples did not stop until they came before the Temple of the Sun, the most beautiful temple in the city. The Saracens honored and revered it more than all the others, because it was a temple to the sun, the noblest of all the planets. At the entrance to this temple there was a very high, beautiful chamber that had been built and established for the peers of the city to hold their courts of justice and business assemblies. This room was called the Seat of Judgment. Joseph and the seventy-five I told you about who were in his group entered this room. They were followed by a large number of the Saracens, [131] who marveled at their strangeness, having never seen such unusual people. Upon entering the room, Joseph found a large number of Saracens, including the lord of the city himself, who was called Evalach the Unknown. He was called the Unknown because no man knew in what country he was born, nor where he came from, nor had they ever had news from anyone who had seen or heard of him in the land. But he was so valiant that through his feats of chivalry he had conquered all the land up to the border of Egypt. And he was still very valiant and courageous, but he was so old that he could not endure the effort of bearing arms. Thus he was no longer as feared or dreaded as he had been in his youth. Rather, the Egyptians were warring against him and had already won a good part of his land that bordered on theirs. No more than three days earlier, they had defeated him in battle, routing him from the battlefield. Because of this, he had sent for all the wise men in his domain, for he wanted to ask their advice about how he might avenge the shame the Egyptians had done to him. At this point, Joseph arrived and heard them discussing the king’s defeat and misfortune. After hearing the truth of the matter, he rejoiced, for he [132] thought that the time had come for his words to be heard and put to work, because of the great need King Evalach had of Our Lord’s help. So he began to thank Our Lord, his Creator, for bringing him there at such a favorable moment. The king had spoken to all his noblemen, and was unable to find help. Rather, they had all failed him, saying they would never again combat the Egyptians, for the latter were far more numerous, and thus only misfortune could befall them. And this was clear, they said, for things had already gone so badly that they did not think it was possible to recoup. As you can hear, they all failed him, urging him to The History of the Holy Grail seek peace!® with the Egyptians, if he could, for they themselves dared not undertake war. This frightened the king so much that he did not know what to say. Then Joseph came before him; seeing him so sad, pale, and pensive, he said, “Evalach, do not be so afraid, for if you believe my advice, you will have joy and victory over your enemies, and glory that will never end.” When Evalach heard this, he looked at him haughtily and said, “Who are you who can give me victory over my enemies and eternal joy?”!! To these words Joseph responded, “By my faith, King [133] Evalach, I did not promise that I would give you victory or eternal joy. But I tell you that if you believe me, you will have victory and joy without end, through the gift and the grace of the One who is powerful over all things.” Evalach answered, “I will gladly listen to your advice. But if you give advice that cannot be believed, the harm will be turned against you.” Joseph replied, “King, this will be advice that will bring honor to the body and profit to the soul, for you will be honored throughout your life, and your soul will be saved after your death.” “Indeed,” said the king, “this advice is not to be refused. Now you can tell me what it is, for if it is as you have said, there is no man in my house I would prefer to listen to. Rather, all the advice you want to give me will be heard.” “King,” said Joseph, “listen then to what I advise. First, you must destroy and break the idols you worship, for you say they are your gods, and you ask them for counsel and help, but they have no power to help you or to injure others. Indeed, you can be sure that they deceived and tricked all your ancestors, for all those who believe these images can help are lost forever if they are still fooled by them on the day of their death. No man should believe that a piece of wood or stone worked by man’s hand could protect him against death or harm; [134] but he should worship the One who suffered the anguish of death on the cross by His own will in order to save and deliver the world from the eternal pain of hell.” “What!” said the king. “Are you telling me that He who suffered the anguish of death, just as you yourself have borne witness, is powerful enough to save me after death, and grant worldly honor? Here I will leave off speaking to you of Joseph and his companions, and we will tell you about King Evalach, who lay in his room, pensive and troubled by two thoughts. The first was the defense of his land against the Egyptians, who had ravaged it terribly and who had defeated and routed him. He was so worried about this that he did not know what to do. He was very much afraid of losing his land and all his worldly honor, because his nobles had all failed him. While he was thinking about these two things* —first one and then the other—a vision came to him. In the middle of his house he saw the trunk of a tall tree, but he could not perceive what kind of tree it was, nor of what nature. From it grew three very large, high, straight limbs, all three of the same size, height, and type, the only difference being that the middle one was covered with an ugly, dark bark, while that of the other two was as clear as crystal. After they had thus mutilated it with the wounds cut all around and the holes made with the augers, a stream of blood came forth so great that everyone who was there could bathe in it, until the tree broke apart. Once it had fallen, nothing was left of it except the outer bark, which remained in a pile. But the wood inside, which was more beautiful, noble, and clear than I could tell or imagine, fell with such force that it flung itself inside the pit where the people had jumped. As the king watched, he saw the tree flung back out of the pit, pulling with it many of the people from the pit, who were holding onto the branches all around. After this, the tree returned to its place and put back on the bark it had had before. But it [158] became completely transformed, turning so clear and resplendent that no man who had looked at it before could believe it was the same bark. Next, the king saw that some of the people who had not jumped into the pit were taking the blood that had flowed onto the ground and were washing their bodies. Once they had done so, their appearance and their faces completely changed. Meanwhile, others were taking the branches and leaves of the tree and breaking up some and burning some. This marvel captured the king’s attention for a long time. It was so wonderful that he was awestruck and believed he was truly asleep and that everything he saw was a dream. Finally he turned over again and again, and realized that in reality he was awake and not dreaming. Then he was even more overwhelmed than he had been before and wondered even more what this marvel could be. After pondering it for a long time, he woke up one of his chamberlains who was sleeping before him and whom he trusted, thinking that he would show this to him alone and that no one else would ever learn about it if he could help it. Thus he denied what he had decided earlier and was so frightened and puzzled that he did not know what to hold as truth: that it was all one tree or that the entire tree was actually three. While he was thinking about this thing that he was thoroughly unable to understand, he looked toward a wall in one of his rooms, where a marble door was set into the wall so artfully that it was barely possible to perceive there was a door or an entrance,’ no matter how attentively one looked. He did not think that anyone in his household knew about it other than himself. As he looked at the door, he saw a small child, who was very handsome and blond, entering, without opening® the door, which remained closed, just as it was before he entered. After a short time he went back out quickly, just as he had entered, without opening the door. Nor was there any evidence [161] that he had either entered or departed. The king was more astonished by this marvel than he had been by all the others, for he believed that neither God nor anyone else could enter through such a strong door or such strong walls without it being apparent in some way. Then the king began to think very intently. The chamberlain who was with him was so frightened that he did not dare utter a word, but lay overwhelmed on the floor, as if he were dead. The king went to him, lifted him up with his right hand, and asked him if he had seen all these marvels and what he thought of them. The man looked at the king as best he could, and when he was able to speak, he said, “Have mercy, my lord! Don’t speak to me about anything, but take me someplace where I won’t see any other marvels like these, for I could not go on living if I saw them.” Thereupon the king took him and led him into a room to go to bed. And all the while he kept thinking about the marvel he had seen—the child who had entered and left the room through the wall. As he went along thinking about this and marveling in his heart about how this could have happened, he heard a voice say to him, “Evalach, what are you marveling at? Just as the child entered the room before your eyes, and just as he left without opening or breaking down the door, thus did the Savior of the world enter the womb of the Virgin Mary without damaging her maidenhead, and thus did He leave.” 6«Trees,” as in Ponceau (Hucher has “branches”). 7 Entrance,” as in Ponceau (Hucher has “window’”). Now let us leave the king, and we will tell about Joseph, who was lying in his bed very pensive and anxious about how he might convert King Evalach to Jesus Christ’s faith. He thought that if the king was not now on the verge of believing, he never would be, for he desperately needed Jesus Christ’s help and wise men’s advice, because he was about to [163] lose the best part or all of his land, most of his noblemen having failed him in his great need. Joseph was thinking so intently about this that he could not sleep; all he did was think. After lying there a long time, neither sleeping or resting, he jumped out of bed. The one you have put on over your tunic symbolizes chastity, for this is a virtue through which the soul, when it leaves the body, departs white and clean and pure, thus harmonizing with all the good things of the soul, that is, with all the qualities it contains. Thus, you must first have chastity inside you, in order to make of it the foundation on which to establish all the other virtues. The other vestment on top of it, which is just as white, symbolizes virginity. Just as virginity cannot be in any place unless chastity be in its company, likewise no priest should put this one on top before putting on the one underneath. This other vestment, which covers the head, symbolizes humility, which is contrary to pride, for pride always goes proudly, with its head raised, but humility goes gently and softly, with head bent. It symbolizes confession; that is why it is completely white, for confession is the whitest thing that exists, since it is the purest. No man is ever so filthy or so poisoned with sin that true confession will not make him completely white and pure. And do you know why it has two horns? Because there are two parts in a confession. The first is repentance, and the second is satisfaction. Repentance is when a man comes to the priest and confesses his sin, completely abandoning it, so that he no longer returns to it. This man comes to repentance, but he is not truly [191] confessed until he makes satisfaction. Satisfaction is when a sinner recognizes his sin, does the penance the priest charges him with, and undergoes the suffering sincerely and with good will. This means that no one can be confessed if he does not have the head and the two limbs of confession: the head is to confess his sin; one of the limbs is to keep from sinning, while the other is to complete the penance imposed. Nor can any man be truly confessed if he fails in any one of these three things. Because confession is the highest thing that exists—the one that repairs®’ in one stroke all the injuries and losses—it is symbolized by this hat, which crowns all the vestments. “Now you are anointed and consecrated, and I have given you the order and rank of bishop to teach My people and honor My New Law. When he started to pull it back,*® he could not, for he felt that it was being put inside his mouth before he could close it. After he had eaten it, it seemed to him. that all the sweet and delectable things one’s tongue could name had entered his body. Next he received part of the holy consecrated drink that was in the chalice. After the angel had taken the dish, another one came and raised the paten on high along with what was on top of it, and carried it with both hands outside of the ark. And the third angel took the chalice and carried it away in the same way after him, while the one carrying the holy dish was last of all. [195] When all three of them had left the ark, so that all the people saw them, a voice spoke and said, “My small people, newly reborn in spiritual birth, I send you your salvation, that is, My body that suffered physical birth and death for you.*® Now take care therefore that you have true faith to receive and eat such a lofty thing, for if you believe perfectly that this is your Savior, you will receive it to the everlasting salvation of the soul. And if you do not believe it completely, you will receive it to the everlasting damnation of the soul and the body. He who eats of My body and drinks of My blood and is not worthy of it, will eat and drink his destruction. Nor can anyone be worthy of it if he is not a true believer. Now take care therefore that you believe it.” Then the angel who was carrying the paten came before Joseph, who knelt and received with joined hands his Savior in visible form, as did each of the others, for it seemed to each one that when the piece in the semblance of bread was put in his mouth, he saw a completely formed child enter his mouth. After he had spoken, a clerk stood up, who was held to be the wisest and the most instructed in their faith. He spoke against Joseph, saying he said nothing, “for if the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit were only one God, none of the three was a complete, perfect God, or else the persons of the Son and of the Holy Spirit had no part in God. No one could reasonably dispute this, for any man who did could not reasonably prove or establish as truth that one of the three persons was a complete deity in itself, once either of the others was mentioned. If it were said that the Holy Spirit was a perfect, complete God, and that the three were only one deity, it would be clear that one was worth as much as the three. After Augustus Caesar had ruled the Roman empire for twenty-seven years, word spread that a man would be born who would conquer the whole world. And it was true, for Jesus Christ, the God of gods and the King of kings, was born in that year. When Augustus Caesar heard the word, as the wise clerks had spread it, though they did not know who this would be, he feared that the lands under the domination of Rome would rise up and overthrow the empire. Because of the certainty of this news, he sent word through all the lands under Roman domination!® that every man and woman should pay a denier!® in recognition that they were subject to Rome. And since France had prouder people than the other lands, [211] he said that from that land they had to send as tribute one hundred knights; one hundred maidens, all daughters of knights; and one hundred male children, five years old or younger. “When the order arrived in France, each city chose according to its status. And this selection was done by lot. Thus it happened that the city of Meaux sent two maidens who were the daughters of Count Sevain. Sevain was count of Meaux and of the surrounding lands. Then the king left with a large company of knights and men-at-arms. They traveled until they reached Tarrabel, where the king waited until his army arrived on the seventh** day. There were more men than had ever been seen together before, and yet none of his leading noblemen came, for they had failed him, as the book recounted earlier.25 On the eighth day the king set out from Tarrabel very early in the morning with his entire army. They rode at a rapid pace straight to Evalachin, where Tholomer lay at siege. This castle [217] called Evalachin had been built by Evalach, and it sat on the most easily defended piece of land any man had ever seen, for it could not be taken by any kind of force other than starvation. It had a gate that no attacking army could control and thereby prevent those on the inside from entering or leaving, for it was*® above the level of dry ground, and underneath it flowed a rapid and torrential river as wide as a bow could shoot an arrow. This gate could not be destroyed by those outside unless they blockaded the city with ships first. But the city could not be blockaded because no fleet hostile to the city’s inhabitants could hold out at close distance for long. The castle was situated in such a way that the foundation was entirely of stone as high as one could throw a rock, with only one gate. At this gate there was enough flat ground so that two carts could enter at once. The flat part was no more than thirty feet long. Thus no man or [218] siege could hold out there, for it was too near the gate, and there was too little room. And the castle above was neither weak nor open, but was completely surrounded by a splendid wall, made entirely of green, beige, and white marble. The tower was four times as high as the walls, and the rock it sat on was the best placed and most unassailable ever seen. On top of this outcrop sat the marble tower, so high that from it one could see the walls of Baghdad gleaming and the river Nile flowing in Egypt. Of such strength and beauty was the castle. And no matter how hot it got in the summertime, the castle’s inhabitants had sweet and cold water from a beautiful and delightful spring that emerged at the foot of the tower. From this spring the?’ stream flowed through a beautiful flat area between the walls of the castle and the tower. It flowed into this area through a copper pipe connected to a marble basin, from which the castle’s residents took the water they needed. This area into which the water flowed through the pipe was the drinking place for the castle’s horses, and it was completely paved with marble and was enclosed by a wall about fifteen feet high. Rather, he won so much earthly honor that all those who saw the battle said that if he alone had not been there, Evalach would certainly have lost his life and his land forever that day, without recourse. But now let us return to the straight road of the story, which says that when Seraphe was joined in battle with the two battalions, so great was the clash of lances on both sides that anyone who heard it without seeing!? it would have thought a great amount of wood was falling. Once the lances were broken, and the knives and fauchards®? and the big sharp steel battle-axes were drawn, there was such a great battle there, and the melee was so deadly on account of the swords, battle-axes, and other metal arms with which?! helmets, shields, and hauberks were struck that it seemed [237] to be a great marvel of blacksmiths. So many limbs were cut off there that no tongue on earth could tell the truth of it unless the One who knows everything revealed it through His Spirit. Now you will hear how this battle ended. Seraphe’s men fought very well at the beginning, but no feat of arms could be compared to his prowess, performed with his hands, for he held a marvelously strong and sharp battle-ax in both hands. And he was tall and big and strong-limbed, with broad shoulders. His arms were large and muscular, while his hands were thin and square. He could spread his legs wide, so he sat very well on horseback. Everywhere he turmed with his battle-ax, having thrown his shield into the press and with the reins over his arms, those he reached were struck so fiercely that they could not recover. That day he struck many a blow, none of which [238] failed to cut an arm, hand, head, or body, either a man’s or a horse’s; he did nothing but marvels. Not much had ever been said about his prowess, so that all those who were watching him marveled. He himself marveled no less than the others, but more, for it did not seem to him that such marvelous prowess could come from such a body as his. And he did not think it came from the One who gave it to him because of Evalach’s prayer, but from the strength of his gods, not realizing they could not help him. He and his men fought well, pushing back the two battalions to where Tholomer was, who was so grieved at seeing his men withdraw that he nearly went out of his mind.”* King Evalach, who was very happy, pointed out to his knights the wonders Seraphe was performing, saying he was the one knight in all the world whose prowess he most wanted to have. When Tholomer saw his men making way for Seraphe and losing more and more ground, he was full of sorrow and shame and sent in two more battalions. Great was the defeat at the passage of the rock, and there were many dead and many captured. But night came, which was disadvantageous to Evalach’s men, and yet they captured and killed so many that not two thousand escaped, between the wounded and unscathed, whereas they had numbered at least sixty thousand at the beginning of the battle. Thus the Egyptians were vanquished by the power of Jesus Christ. Evalach returned to Orcaut with his men, who had won so much booty that even the poorest and weakest expected it would make them rich and comfortable. And when he entered the [264] city, he found it so full of bound prisoners and the men guarding them that no one could take a step. He came back out and had tents and pavilions set up in the beautiful meadow outside the city. There he and his men camped. Josephus replied that he cared little about an oath made upon her idols, for they could neither harm nor help her; and that he cared little about her faith, for she had none, since she did not believe in the faith, that is, in Jesus Christ, [266] who is all faith and all belief. He then began to tell her the articles of faith and of the Trinity. She looked at him and asked him his name, and he said he was called Josephus by his baptismal name. “Josephus,” she said, “the fact is there isn’t any man who can teach me about this.” Then she ordered everyone to withdraw, and immediately began to ask Josephus if he wished to discuss it. She was a Christian without the knowledge of my father, or of anyone in her lineage except me, and I will tell you how it happened. In the hearing of everyone there, he said, “King, you saw three trees in your palace, and it was right here in this place. These three trees were of the same girth and height and appearance, except that the one in the middle was covered with a very ugly, black bark. The one with the black bark was the symbol of the Son of God, that is, Jesus Christ, who covered Himself on earth with ugly mortal flesh, and the other two symbolized the Father and the Holy Spirit. The kind of people who were under the Father symbolized the beginning of the world, for at this time the Trinity was not yet known. The two who left the company of the others and jumped into the pit symbolized the first man and woman, who went to hell as soon as they died. All the others followed, for after that there was no one, no matter how much good he did during [315] his life, who did not go to hell as soon as the soul left the body, until the time came when the Son of God suffered death. The rock was on this route, and it was so high that one could survey the entire Western sea® as far as those places where land could be found. The rock was as high as you have heard, and it was in the wildest and least frequented place that exists among habitable sites at sea. This place was so uncultivated and unpleasant that there was no earthly sustenance there at all, not even a handful of friable soil. Rather, it consisted entirely of raw stone, up to the edge of the sea. Because the rock sat in such a wild and perilous place, the people living around there called it the Rock of the Perilous Port.4 And long ago [340] a pirate called Foucaire built a very proud house there. This pirate was unusually large and so strong that no man could hold out against the strength of his limbs. The pirate came to this rock, and he made his home out of the rock itself, which he dug out until he had a house that could lodge twenty men. In this lodging he and his numerous companions stayed, but they could not all® sleep inside the rock, for they numbered a good ninety, and sometimes there were one hundred or more. So they siept beyond the rock in their galleys, which were at all times prepared for them. During the night when it was very dark, they put great brands of burning fire on the rock. Often those who came there, such as merchants or other people passing by, did not escape without peril, for it often happened that the ships ran up against the rock so hard that they broke up,® and the pirates were ready to attack them with their galleys. Thus they fell upon two dangers, for some were drowned, while others were killed when they thought they had reached safety. For a long time the pirate led his disgraceful life in this way, until it happened that the great Pompey, who [341] was the Roman emperor at that time, crossed the sea of Greece and came into the land of Syria. After he had gone throughout the lands of the East and captured the defended fortresses as far as Babylon, he heard about these pirates who thus killed everyone who passed there. And then he said that everything he had done was for naught if he did not rid the land of this pirate. After a good part of the night had passed, they set out and went along until they came close enough to the rock to throw a stone by hand. When the pirates heard therm coming, they boarded their galleys and prepared to assault them. The men steering Pompey’s ship knew the narrows of the rock, so they did not try [342] to head straight toward the fire but went to the side of it, thus blocking a galley between them and the rock and causing it to run against the rock so hard that it broke up completely and flew into pieces. This grieved him so much that he nearly went out of his mind. And if he were killed in this way, the empire would be greatly dishonored by the fact that the pirates had killed the emperor. Pompey sent forty knights forward and had them light the fire with pieces of ships that had broken up on the rock, which were plentiful. When the fire had caught well, the flames shot up to the entrance of the cave where the pirates were, and much of the smoke went in. Upon seeing this, the pirates took fresh water, which they had in abundance, went out, and poured it onto the fire, which became so full of smoke that it was nearly extinguished. However, those below shot numerous arrows and threw stones at the pirates, wounding four of them. When the thieves saw the injuries inflicted on their side, they withdrew into the cave, but there they were more uncomfortable than outside, for so much smoke filled the cave that they could not see a thing. Realizing they could not endure it, they all went out and did what they could to put the fire out. The knights attacked them, fighting them boldly, and the thieves defended themselves fiercely, [346] despite having been injured and wounded. The melee lasted a long time, and many were wounded on both sides. When Pompey saw that the enemy were holding out so long, he was grieved; he immediately ran up to the fire, where the thieves had already descended to put it out, and he himself pursued them so fiercely that they did not dare to wait for him. They fled back up into the cave, with Pompey rushing after them, along a narrow path cut into the rock, for there was no other way to go. The cave was in such a steep place that no one could reach it except by the path, which was cut into the solid rock. And yet the cave was not at the highest point on the rock, but on one of the sides, in the widest part. And the entrance was so low and narrow that only one man could enter at a time, and he had to do so sideways. The king felt this great heat, and if he had been uncomfortable before, his pain and his discomfort now increased a hundred times. Suffering from the heat, he saw the ship ready before him, where he could go if he wished to avoid the sun. But he feared the anger of his Lord, for he was ready to suffer death rather than leave the rock. For a long time he suffered this painful heat—so long that his strength of heart failed him, and he was so weak that he could no longer bear up. So he fainted, falling face down and lying for a long time on the ground like someone who has lost his hearing, his feeling, and his sight. When he came to, he lifted his head a little to find out if the heat was still as great as before. And when he saw that the day had become temperate and the air sweet and mild, as it should between the hours of nones and vespers, and that the heat had dissipated, he was very happy. Then he tried to see if he could stand up, despite the weakness of his head. As he started to get up, he felt no pain in his head or any of his other limbs. Thereupon he sat up and began to marvel] at the great adventures that had befallen him, wondering what they could mean, for it seemed to him that he had undergone extremely great pain and then felt nothing. [396] He marveled so much that he thought it was a dream, and yet at the same time he remembered all the adventures that had happened to him, just as you have heard. Thus he thought and reflected in his heart. Meanwhile the day passed so that it began to get dark. Then he looked far out to sea, and saw a ship coming. It was so beautiful and impressive that never in his life had he seen one so richly and beautifully appointed. The ship came on very rapidly and noisily; once it had come closer to him, he saw two shields hanging at the two windows of the beautiful little forecastle at the prow. He recognized the two shields: one was his and the other belonged to his brother-in-law Nascien. At that moment all his blood drained away, so frightened was he. And he began to think so intently that he completely lost himself in thought. While he was plunged in thought, the ship approached; in it a horse began to whinny and neigh and stamp its feet so violently that it seemed to him the entire ship would break apart and capsize. The king listened to the horse and recognized it by the whinnying. He knew for sure that it was his horse, the one he had won from Tholomer in the battle at Orcaut. He was able to recognize it because [397] its whinny was different from that of any other horse, and it was also different in other ways. He wondered how the horse and the shields had thus come to a foreign place. The ship then reached the rock, and the king stood up to see what kind of people were inside. As he looked, he saw a great many very handsome 68 people; then he saw a man who seemed to be a knight come forth. When he was nearby, the king recognized him as one of his knights, the brother of his seneschal, the one who had been killed in the battle against Tholomer. When the knight saw him, he greeted him, looking very unhappy. The king ran quickly to embrace him and asked him why he looked so sad. The knight answered, “Oh, my lord, because I bring you terrible news, which will make your heart grieve, and it will not be surprising if you are saddened and chagrined by it. And be assured that we have had many difficulties and travails in our search for you since we left your land.” “What!” said the king. “What have J lost then?” “Indeed, my lord,” said he, “you have lost the best of all your friends, your brother-in-law Nascien, [398] who is lying dead in this ship.” Upon hearing this, the king fainted, falling flat on the ground. When he came to, he asked to see Nascien, crying out terribly, like a man who has lost his senses. The man who had told him the news raised him up, took him by the left hand, and led him into the ship, while he grieved so much that he nearly killed himself. Once on board, the king saw the bier and ran straight to it. He lifted the rich cloth covering it and saw Nascien’s face and appearance as clearly as ever. He fainted again, losing consciousness so completely that those who saw him did not think he would escape without dying or being wounded. When he stood up, wishing to ask the knight how this had happened, he looked back toward the rock and saw he was so far away that he could hardly see it. Thereupon, he was so grief-stricken that he could not utter a word, but fell back into a faint before the bier. When he came to, he crossed himself. At once he saw no man or woman, nor the bier in the ship. And then he began to sob bitterly, saying, “Oh, dear Lord God, I have so badly kept watch! [399] I can see that You are angry with me, and I have indeed deserved it.” Suddenly, he saw at the prow of the ship the man from the beautiful ship who had spoken the good words to him all week. He despaired, saying, “Oh, my lord, I have been tricked by the one you told me to watch out for! You certainly told the truth when you said that the devil would take me from the rock with his left hand.” And then he began to cry and grieve. The man said to him, “Don’t cry so much. Be quiet and avoid doing worse, for you certainly need to.” And the king said, “Oh, dear sir, you who know all things, for God’s sake, tell me what I should do and how I should act.” The man replied, “A number of terrifying adventures will befall you. Do not drink or eat anything until you see Nascien, your brother-in-law, come to you as a good and true Christian. As soon as you see him acting as a Christian should, you can be sure that your deliverance has come. Nascien's imprisonment hard and cruel. ‘Nascien was placed in the depths of a dangerous, black, very dark cell, removed from the company and solace of any people. He ate and drank litle. He could not use any of his limbs, for his hands and feet were in chains; at all times he was in the same state, never taking off his clothes or shoes but lying day and night in them. Once Galafre had imprisoned Nascien in such a terrible place, he sought to torment him further and succeeded in imprisoning one of Nascien’s young sons, who was only seven years and five months old. This child was very handsome and seemed to be descended from a noble family and high lineage. At his birth a great and unusual marvel occurred in the city of Orberica. He was born on a beautiful summer day, around noon, on the second day of the month of June. At the time he was born, the sun, which should have been at its brightest and hottest, suddenly appeared just as clearly as in the morning when it rises, while the moon and the stars were seen as Clearly as if it were night. This certainly meant that he would probe and learn? all the properties of the heavens. When the men who had found him raised him and saw him in such a state, they were very much afraid, for he could not say a word or open his eyes, so they believed in truth that he was dead. Now the story says that after Nascien was put in Galafre’s prison, and his son was imprisoned with him and all his land seized, his wife, who was a young and very noble woman—the daughter of the king of the Midians—was exiled from her land. The lady was so beautiful that everyone who saw her considered the beauty of her figure and face sovereign over that of all women. Besides being beautiful, she also possessed good traits, for she was generous toward God, gracious to people on earth, and simple, faithful, and chaste toward her husband. And she loved him so much that nothing could make her heart joyful unless she knew first that her husband’s heart was content. [419] The lady was such as you have heard, and her name was Flegetine. When she learned that her husband and lord was in prison, you can be sure that she lamented and grieved. In the midst of her great sorrow, the nobles of the kingdom sent word to her to relinquish all her land. On that day she was at Orberica, the main seat of the duchy. She relinquished it willingly because she thought her lord would thereby be released from prison, but Galafre’s counsel did not allow this, just as the story recounted earlier. When she saw that the affair had gone so far that she would have neither her lord nor her land, she was more sorrowful than before. Then the lady went to the home of a vavasor, an old man of great loyalty, who had always been her son’s tutor. The lady had always had great affection for him and had often given him and his wife gifts. It seemed to her that she would find greater love in him than in any other because she had raised him from great poverty to great riches, and so she had greater confidence in him. The duchess Flegetine went to this vavasor’s home, very sorrowful and distraught. Rather, she said, “My lady, I have come to the home of a man whom I have found the most loyal in the world. He is one of my vavasors, and be assured that his heart would be very chagrined if I were to give up his company at this point. I will not leave him, my lady, for since he accompanied me at the beginning of my exile, I should indeed accompany him when God grants the restoration of my joy and my rank. And I will suffer less chagrin and sorrow here than I would if I were with you, for each time we saw each other, our sorrow would immediately be renewed.” The queen took great pains to try to find a way to take her sister-in-law with her, but Flegetine did not want to leave the vavasor despite any of her prayers. Thus, in sorrow and distress, the queen departed, and Flegetine remained, grieving unceasingly. Indeed, her tears and sorrows grew deeper each day. For a long time the lady led [422] this life without anyone being able to comfort her until the day came when Nascien, her lord, escaped, and her son also. When she had news of that, she began to be a little comforted and appeared more cheerful than before. On the seventh night? after Nascien escaped from prison, it happened that she lay slumbering in her bed, not having slept in a long time, and she was now beginning to rest. And yet it seemed to her it could not have any truth in it. That morning she went first of all to Holy Church to worship. This island was rightly called turning because it is true that it turned. But everyone who has heard about it does not know how it turns, and it is right that this story show the truth, for if it did not clearly show the reason and knowledge about every doubtful thing it mentions, it would only be words interlaced together, just like some people who speak many words, claiming their truth, but who cannot cite any support, except that they have heard it from others. This story eschews this bad way, for it does not set forth any doubtful statement [429] without explaining it with utter clarity. That is why it is rightly called the Chronicle of Chronicles. Now the chronicle stops to recount the true ways of the island where Nascien was carried, which the local people call, as I told you, the Turning Isle. It is proven truth that at the beginning of all things, when the Founder of the world divided and parted the four elements, which had all been piled up in one mass, and separated? heaven, which is full of all light and purity, and which the Scripture calls fire, from the other three, He established it in the highest place, for He made it cover and enclose all the others. Because heaven and air and earth and water had once been a single mass, each one, even though they were all of clashing natures, was inevitably* bound up with the others and linked according to its particular properties, heaven being by nature hot and light, and earth by nature cold and heavy. And so anyone can understand that heaven felt to some extent the cold of the earth or water, and these two likewise felt to some extent heaven’s great heat. [430] Thus you can understand the clashes among them; they were harmful to one other and could not bear one another. Because the earth, which is heavy and cold and a mass of filth, touched heaven, which is light and hot and the source of all purity, it happened that heaven gathered up filth in the form of masses of iron slag from earth as well as rusty matter from water. But when the Sovereign Father, who is the source of all knowledge, had separated one from the other and disjoined them, He placed heaven in its true honor and led it to purity, for He made it clear and shining and light and full of all warmth, while He left the earth cold and heavy, making it a mass of every heavy thing. In a sector of this sea, which lies between this island and this port, there is a great deal of lodestone, or magnetic iron ore, down on the bottom. You heard earlier that the story says the earth in the mass was iron slag; now this stone called lodestone has the property of liking iron above all and readily pulls it close. Once the iron is next to it and can join its force to it, it is not easy to separate it, the strength of the stone pulls the iron so much that it makes it touch it, unless there is more iron than stone or some other thing that can overcome the force of the magnet. Its ribs possess such power that if any man takes one, as long as he holds it, he will not remember any of the joys or sorrows he has had except the one thing that caused him to take the rib. As soon as he puts it down, he will think again just as he is accustomed to, according to human nature. The two ribs in the sword’s hilt have these powers and these qualities. And no matter how full of faith and belief he may be, let him not be changeable, like the [491) pennant that turns where the wind blows it. The Christian should be just like the strong tower, built sturdily on a good foundation, fearing no siege or assault by its neighbor. The Christian should hold just as firmly to the virtues of Holy Church, so that the devil, who watches day and night to snatch man away from good thoughts and works, happens by chance to approach him, he may find him strong, holding firm, and well established on the good rock called Jesus Christ. “Just as ships were first built so that one might cross the water without danger and come ashore safely, in the same way Holy Church was built to sustain the Christian in this world, which is symbolized by water, so that he may not perish while he wanders in this earthly life, which is poor, sorrowful, and full of suffering. By the ship you should understand Holy Church, and by the sea, the world. And just as the ship carries man on the sea without danger and bears him on the water, thus Holy Church bears her servant among the filth and sins of the world, [492] so that he may not be sullied, debased, or stained with mortal sin. Holy Church makes her good servant, her good minister, rise above all sins, clean and purged of all baseness, just as gold that is refined seven times emerges pure above all other metals, and just as the sun appears in splendor above all the stars. “Now that I have told you what the ship symbolizes and what you should understand by it, I will tell you what the bed inside the ship symbolizes. The bed, which was so splendid and well adorned with marvelous and excellent things, symbolizes the holy table where the Son of God is consecrated every day, when the wine changes into blood and the bread into true flesh through the high and holy words commemorated there by the mouth of the blessed person who undertakes this office. By the bed you should understand the Holy Cross, where the Son of God, in [493] His graciousness, allowed Himself to suffer, in order to redeem the human race from eternal sorrow, for by sinning mortally, day after day, more and more, humanity had fallen into the darkness of hell. You should understand the bed as the sign of solace and rest; in this way the bed should be compared, though unequally, to the cross, as a similar thing. In the same way that, after the fatigue of work, every earthly man seeks rest in a bed, likewise you should understand that after the fatigue and travail of the great anguish of hell, the human race took rest and solace in the generous gift the Son of God made of Himself, on the True Cross, on the very day He suffered death in order to remove sinners from the sorrowful prison. “I have explained the symbolism of the ship and the bed you saw inside. Patience is symbolized by the emerald, which is green in all seasons. And this stone rightly symbolizes this quality, for just as it is always green,!° likewise you can see that patience is always verdant and forceful so that it cannot be moved either by adversity or misfortune once it is well rooted in the Christian’s heart. Similarly, he in whom it is housed achieves victory, for you know very well that one cannot vanquish one’s enemy so well as by forbearance. “The bed was encompassed and enclosed by these three things, the first of which is called virginity, the second charity, and the third patience. And well it should be, since it is the symbol of the True Cross, where the Son of God was struck with the anguish of death. It is clear that He did not lack these three things, for it is well known and truth attests that the three virtues—virginity, charity, and patience—kept Him [495] company during the anguish He suffered. Celidoine’s Adventures at Sea.! Now the the Story of the Holy Grail says here that after King Label’s men had seized Celidoine, they took him among the rocks [534] to their pavilions. And when they realized they could do nothing else, they said to each other that since they had in their power the one who had caused them this sorrow, they would take their revenge on him. Some of them thought they should kill Celidoine, while others said he was still too young a child and that they should be avenged? some other way. Everywhere they went they asked for news of Nascien, but they never found anyone who could give them information, and that frightened them. When they had long been in foreign countries, in pagan as well as other lands, it seemed to them that they would not hear news of Nascien, either near or far, and that they had left their country for naught, for they would not find what they were seeking. One night it happened that they were lodged at the home of a pagan vavasor, a very worthy man in his religion. In the evening after they had eaten, their host asked them where they were from and where [11] they were going. They said they were from Sarras and were seeking their lord, who was called Nascien and who had disappeared through the most marvelous adventure in the world. “What!” he exclaimed. “You are Christians?” They replied that this was true. “And how is it,” he asked, “that you were so bold as to hurry straight into the land of the Saracens, knowing very well that they hate you mortally, since you oppose their faith and belief?” “Dear sir,” said one of them, “distress and anguish to find what we are seeking made us forge ahead, for we don’t know if our lord is among pagans or Christians. The Story of Hippocrates: His Powers, His Trouble with Women, and His Downfall. Now the story says it is true—and the Chronicle of the Philosophers attests to it—that Hippocrates was the foremost practitioner of the art of medicine, of all the men who were dominant in his time and who had worked long and diligently at this science. Because of something he did in Rome his knowledge was recognized and tested, and since then he has been [30] held in great esteem by philosophers and called paramount? doctor. And I will tell you how this happened. It is proven truth that in the time of the good emperor Augustus Caesar, Hippocrates came to Rome. At the moment he entered the city, it happened that he found great sorrow there, on all sides, as if everyone saw his child dead before him. He was astounded when he saw everyone mourning so deeply, so he asked a child he met to tell him the reason for this grief. The child replied, “We are grieving because the emperor’s nephew, who was healthy last night, is now dead. He was such a beautiful child and so valorous that all Rome is diminished by his death. This is the reason for our sorrow.” “Where is the body?” asked Hippocrates. “My lord,” said the [31] child, “it is in our emperor’s hall.” After hearing this, Hippocrates left the child and headed for the palace, thinking that if he could arrive in time, before the soul had left, he had learned enough to bring him back to health through his medicine. Upon arriving, he pushed through all the people until he came to the body. They were all so intent on their grief that no one attempted to keep him away. When he came to the body, he began to iuspect that part where he might learn whether the child was dead. Thus it happened that as soon as he had put his hands on the body, he knew the soul was still in it. Then he opened the mouth and put inside it a liquor made from herbs of such great power and strength that the child immediately got up [32] as healthy and well as ever. When the emperor saw this, he ran to Hippocrates to embrace him and welcome him, and the others did likewise. As a reward for his service, the emperor offered him whatever he requested, if it was something he could give. The emperor asked him his name, and he said it was Hippocrates. “I know very well,” said the emperor, “by the fact that you have the power to bring a dead man to life, that you are the wisest clerk and the best philosopher who has ever existed. I will therefore do you such honor that it will be talked about forever.” Then he had a golden statue made, as tall as a man and as similar as one could make it to Hippocrates’s form. But she was lying about this, for the emperor’s son was not imprisoned there, nor was the vessel used to bear food. It served another purpose, which was very shameful, for when a man was sentenced to death, he was immediately put in the vessel and pulled up on high by this very rope, until he was nearly as high as the battlements, where he was left without being moved for a day and a night, until the Romans and people from all around had seen him. Once he had been there long enough to serve this purpose, he was lowered and was then beaten throughout the city. Thus the vessel was commonly called the Vessel of Judgment. Nor was anyone ever put in it for [46] any reason, unless he had been convicted of thievery or murder or some other base crime. The next day it happened that the emperor arose so early to go hunting that before day broke he and all his men were already in the forest, leaving no one in the palace.!4 In the morning, when the Romans arose and left their dwellings, they looked at the tower and saw there was a man in the wooden vessel. They immediately thought that it was one of the criminals of Rome who had been caught and sentenced to death. They looked until they recognized Hippocrates. And when they discovered [49] that it was truly he, they were astonished. “Now what can he have done?” they asked. “You can be very sure that he has committed a worse offense than any other man; otherwise, the emperor would not have had him placed in the Vessel of Judgment.” That day they repeatedly asked why he had been put in such a place. But he was so grief-stricken and ashamed that he did not dare look at them, nor did he have the courage to respond. And they truly believed that the emperor himself had had him put there and that Hippocrates had committed such a crime that he had been sentenced to death by the court’s common assent, for if they had not thought this, he would not have remained there so long. All day long Hippocrates stayed in this way in the vessel that was only used to hold criminals. All the Romans went to see him and [50] look at him more than they would any other man who was put there, because he was so close to the emperor and considered to be so wise. Those in the tower were not bold enough to remove him, for they truly believed the emperor had had him placed there. Thus he remained there all day. In the evening, when the emperor returned from the forest and dismounted, he saw that the vessel contained! a man. He asked who it was and for what misdeed he had been put there. “My lord,” said those with him, “that is Hippocrates, the philosopher whom you have honored so much and whom you used to love so much.” “What has he done wrong?” asked the emperor. “My lord, we don’t know.” “Who put him there?” said the emperor. “My lord, we don’t know,” they replied. “Have him removed at once,” said the [51] emperor. “If the philosophers put him there without my leave, I will make them repent it.” Those to whom he had given orders went immediately to the tower and lowered the vessel; they removed Hippocrates and brought him before the emperor. Nascien and his wife sent far and wide for news of Joseph of Arimathea and his followers, thinking Celidoine was with them. But at this point they heard nothing, despite the efforts of the men they sent.* It grieved them, and several times when they were together they said that Joseph® should come visit them or request words of comfort that might make them more hopeful and content. They were downcast and silent all the time, waiting to see whether God might send them news of their child. They went about day and night with such sad faces that Nascien became withdrawn, completely losing his desire to eat or drink, day or night. He was intent only on praying to Our Lord, in His sweet pity, to make some sign that he knew where Josephus and Celidoine were; “and, dear Lord God, I pray to you not to let me die except where they will pass away and in the very land that our household is to multiply and increase.” His wife Flegetine had told him the dream she had had: how she was told she should go to the land that would be increased by her household.‘ [104] Nascien made this prayer day and night. Then he dressed and got ready and went to the stable, where he took a good strong horse. He managed to lead it out of the stable so quietly that no one noticed it. Once he was beyond the gate, he mounted and set out on his way toward the sea as directly as he could. At the time he left the castle it was very cold, and it was snowing so hard that the ground was completely covered with snow, so that he would not have known how to hold to his path if it had not been for the moon, which was shining clearly and serenely. Thus Nascien left the castle, never to return. All night long he rode as straight as possible toward the sea, in order to leave his land and reach the sea. The next day, when his wife awoke and did not find her husband beside her, she began at once to grieve so bitterly that everyone gathered to ask what they could do. But first he dismounted and tied his horse to an olive tree. Then he went quickly toward the melee. When the giant saw him coming with his sword drawn, he tried to jump up but could not, for Nascien, who recognized Nabor, held the giant with all his strength.
